We contend that prior studies on coreference resolution have overlooked a fundamental issue: the fundamental assumption of Centering Theory (CT; Grosz et al., 1995) regarding local discourse coherence. CT asserts that the set of entities mentioned in an utterance constitutes its "center," a concept thought to ensure local coherence. Since CT relies on a unique center per utterance, we examine coreference systems through the lens of a simplified, coreference-aware version of the theory we term "Flat Centering Theory" (FCT). Our research demonstrates a widespread failure of FCT in contemporary coreference systems. We instrumentalized a set of coreference features representing coreference patterns, which we use to quantify a system's adherence to a version of CT we define as "Nested Centering Theory." We found that coreference features account for less variance in performance than system-specific coreference features, and that systems performing similarly in terms of FCT compliance also exhibit comparable performance differences in coreference features. Consequently, we conclude that coreference systems operate without regard for discourse structure, a finding that aligns with recent observations about the decentralized nature of discourse features (Berant et al., 2017). This research examines the automated derivation of application-specific code from product-line models, with a primary focus on improving the understandability and modularity of the resulting applications. The proposed framework, referred to as CONFISS (Configuration Instance Synthesis), is built upon the concept of configuration patterns. These patterns represent recurring groups of feature interactions that define valid configuration subspaces, thereby facilitating the organization of complex interaction complexes into a hierarchical structure. This approach distinguishes feature interactions by their scope: pattern for products, modules, and components. Furthermore, the framework accounts for conditional compile-time and runtime behavior, as well as constant expressions, within each configuration instance.

This research investigates the automated configuration of software product lines (SPLs) modeled using feature models, aiming to generate standalone code for specific product configurations while preserving the ability to trace this code back to the original feature model. The core component of the proposed framework, named CONFISS, is the configuration pattern. These patterns are logical formulas comprising SMT fragments that capture constraint combinations relevant to specific SPLs. The framework leverages the capabilities of an SMT solver to automatically generate configuration-specific code.

The core contribution of this thesis is the development of the CONFISS framework, which enables the automated generation of software products from feature models through the use of configuration patterns. The name 'CONFISS' is a portmanteau of CONFIGURATION INSTANCE SYNTHESIS. Within this framework, a software product is created by combining implementation code directly provided by developers with automatically synthesized code derived from the feature model. The automatic synthesis process involves two primary phases: filtering and binding. The binding process, which is the focal point of this work, utilizes an SMT solver

WiFi fingerprinting, which involves gathering Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) measurements at known locations, is a prevalent technique in various positioning algorithms found in existing literature. However, accurately calculating the spatial distance between fingerprints is highly dependent on the choice of signal distance function used to map signal space to geospatial distance. This study proposes leveraging machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between fingerprints. To do this, we developed a novel geospatial distance dataset and introduced a new position estimation problem: learning the geospatial distance metric from this data. Our analysis shows that the learning task is challenging due to the complex, non-linear nature of the WiFi channel and significant variability in signal propagation across different indoor environments. To address these challenges, we constructed a comprehensive dataset featuring diverse signal propagation characteristics. We evaluated multiple learning algorithms, with support vector regression (SVR) showing the most promise. Based on various performance metrics, our results indicate that an online SVR algorithm outperforms other methods in generalization ability. Finally, we established an upper bound for WiFi fingerprint-based position estimation. Finally, we set a ceiling for the accuracy of this estimation method.

Accuracy, which involves both correctness and precision, is the primary concern when locating individuals and devices. This paper introduces a novel framework for understanding and classifying location accuracy using a matrix of correctness and precision factors. This matrix highlights that certain accuracy types, specifically those in the top-right quadrant, have been largely overlooked in current research. These "precise but incorrect" locations are areas of intense interest for future study. To fill this gap, we developed a location system that can generate positions of varying degrees of correctness and precision. To explore this, we analyzed the factors influencing correctness and precision, such as sensor noise, the number of sensors, and the geometry of the setup. We also examined how the size of the search area (generated via Gaussian processes) correlates with precision. Furthermore, we investigated how different position-estimation algorithms can be tuned to produce positions with different accuracy characteristics. Finally, we applied this framework to classify location-system accuracy in prior research. This framework helps researchers and engineers understand existing systems, identify areas for improvement, and design new solutions that balance correctness and precision as needed. The core findings of this study are summarized in a location accuracy database.

are governed by Service Level Agreements (SLAs), necessitating rigorous monitoring to ensure compliance. A common approach utilizes agent-based methods where periodic measurements yield data interpreted into service state information. This paper examines the problem of optimizing the timing of these measurements to minimize a specified cost function. We formulate the challenge of determining an optimal schedule for network services as a Combinatorial Optimization (CO) problem. We introduce two algorithms to solve this CO problem: a novel Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Linear Programming (LP) relaxation solved via the Interior Point Method (IPM). The proposed algorithms address two objective functions: minimizing the count of consecutive incorrect service states and maximizing service state verification. The study presents a formal definition of the problem, details the two algorithms, and reports on numerical experiments aimed at evaluating their computational efficiency. Results indicate that the LP-based approach is optimal for networks comprising up to a few dozen links. For larger-scale networks, the proposed GA demonstrates superior performance, offering up to a 100-fold improvement in computation time compared to LP. These findings underscore the potential of using a genetic algorithm to solve service measurement scheduling problems in extensive networks.

Consequently, a strategic selection of filling patterns can substantially elevate the onset of beam breakup instability, thereby broadening the operational utility of future ERLs. Beam breakup instability, first predicted in linear accelerators over eight decades ago, remains partially theoretical regarding its application to high-gradient superconducting RF structures used in ERLs. This work provides a comprehensive analysis of the instability's dependence on charge, frequency, machine length, and coupling impedance, alongside an investigation into the influence of filling patterns. Furthermore, we extend the standard formalism to derive a general expression applicable to various filling patterns and incorporate a multi-bunch treatment that accounts for all upstream currents acting on individual bunches or, alternatively, the cumulative effect of a single bunch on all upstream bunches within a fill. Through these approaches, we achieve a complete understanding of the early stages of beam-RF interaction, including the temporal evolution of beam current and the modulation of bunches or entire filling patterns. Additionally, we formulate a criterion for the filling-pattern-dependent threshold current, which is validated against results from beam breakup instability simulations. precision long-baseline experiments depend on accurate models of neutrino-nucleus interactions, which currently represent a significant source of systematic uncertainty due to the historical inability of detectors to observe final-state neutrons. Three-dimensional projection scintillator trackers, integral to the near detectors of next-generation long-baseline facilities, offer a solution. Their fine granularity and excellent timing resolution enable the measurement of neutron kinetic energy on an event-by-event basis, providing crucial data to refine interaction models and neutrino energy reconstruction methods. Two prototypes were exposed to the neutron beamline at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) in 2019 and 2020, covering neutron energies from 0 to 800 MeV. To validate neutron detection capabilities, the total neutron-scintillator cross section was measured and compared against external data. The resulting total cross section for scintillator in the 98 to 688 MeV range is determined to be 0.36 ± 0.05 barn. These findings support the development of comprehensive neutron interaction models, which are essential for enhancing the accuracy of neutrino-nucleus interaction models in future neutrino experiments. To demonstrate the utility of 3PTs for neutron detection, the resolution of neutrino energy reconstruction was evaluated in a signal-rich configuration of the DUNE Near Detector. Without neutron detection, the 3$\sigma$ band of the neutrino energy spectrum misreconstructs by up to 100 MeV for neutrons exceeding 200 MeV; this issue is significantly mitigated with 3PT data. We introduce a neutron-reconstruction algorithm that achieves a detection efficiency of $\mathcal{A}=92.4\%$ and a purity of $94.4\%$ for neutrons with kinetic energy greater than 100 MeV. For neutrons with energy above 200 MeV, the pure-sample detection efficiency is $86.6\%$, while the efficient-sample detection efficiency is $96.2\%$. The 3PT scintillator total cross section is approximately 16 times smaller than the neutron-proton cross section, confirming that neutron scattering off nucleons within the target material dominates the interaction cross section. Finally, the 3PT scintillator total cross section was parameterized using an empirical formula for neutrons with energy exceeding 125 MeV.

micrometer-sized chondritic grains vary with temperature, revealing a fivefold reduction in surface energy as temperature rises. This study investigates the influence of surface water. While ambient lab conditions feature multiple water layers, protoplanetary discs at low pressure and moderate temperatures likely retain only a monolayer, which evaporates entirely as dust migrates inward into hotter zones. To model this, we measured the tensile strength of chondritic material using two new preparation techniques alongside our previous methods: air-dried cylinders and vacuum-heated cylinders (super-dry). For temperatures up to 1000 K, dry samples exhibited sticking forces approximately ten times greater than wet ones. Super-dry samples mirrored the dry samples' behavior up to 900 K, but beyond that point, their sticking forces rose exponentially, reaching another factor of ~100 near 1200 K. This enhancement from wet to dry conditions extends a trend previously observed in amorphous silicates and multimineral mixtures. Consequently, super-dry dust findings suggest that aggregate growth is significantly amplified in a narrow high-temperature region around 1200 K, potentially representing an optimal zone for planetesimal formation. These results aid high-precision numerical models in pinpointing where micron-sized discs transition into planetary inventory. Furthermore, the spatial distribution of sticking forces suggests that primordial asteroids should display an unexpected internal structure: a central core formed at ~1200 K, characterized by higher density, magnetic susceptibility, and a metallic composition of roughly 50%.

Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic/dynamic limitations, recent advancements in constrained imitation learning enable the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings, thereby expanding the method's applicability. Although various constraints such as joint limits, obstacle avoidance, and planar restrictions have been explored, nonlinear hard constraints remain insufficiently addressed. This paper introduces Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) to tackle core challenges in imitation learning, particularly nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP learns probabilistic patterns from multiple demonstrations, adapts skills to new environments, ensures continuity and differentiability, and effectively handles both linear and nonlinear equality and inequality constraints. Furthermore, the paper examines the application of EKMP in parallel computing. Comprehensive numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy. The study concludes that EKMP is a robust framework for imitation learning, capable of overcoming limitations found in current state-of-the-art techniques. In the standard single-objective scenario, combining EKMP with a secondary objective function allows for the handling of hybrid constraints that include random parameters. Finally, a motion planning case involving a two-degree-of-freedom robot arm demonstrates the successful handling of all discussed constraint types, with experimental validation confirming the algorithm's reliability. This research underscores the significant potential of EKMP for future research directions in EKMP and generally for nonlinear control systems.

While the NLO kernel has been computed, its full expression remains unverified; currently, only the forward scattering limit has been compared against data from particle colliders. Conversely, although a formal expression for the NNLO anomalous dimension has been derived, it has never been compared to collider measurements, which are strictly the domain of QCD perturbation theory. To enable such a comparison, we present a Python code that evaluates the NNLO anomalous dimension for any rapidity gap size and transverse momentum. Our numerical comparison with experimental data demonstrates that the NNLO anomalous dimension significantly influences rapidity evolution at extremely small transverse momenta, below $1~GeV$. Furthermore, we show that incorporating the NNLO anomalous dimension is essential for extrapolating to the LHC beam energy in certain processes involving rapidity gaps. Finally, we estimate the energy scale of the tau lepton collider beyond which the comparison between the full NNLO kernel and the resummation utilizing the NNLO anomalous dimension becomes necessary.

This letter introduces a formal expression for the NNLO anomalous dimension within the momentum-space BFKL equation. In this study, we employ quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation to investigate the superconducting behavior of a doped two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model incorporating Rashba spin-orbit coupling within a Zeeman field. Our results generally indicate that Rashba coupling promotes s-wave superconductivity. Specifically, when a finite Zeeman field suppresses superconductivity via Pauli pair-breaking, the Rashba interaction mitigates the resulting spin polarization by mixing spins, thereby restoring superconductivity at finite temperatures. We attribute this advantageous effect to a spin-flip mechanism that enhances the probability of electron pair propagation in time-reversed states. Furthermore, an analysis of the Fermi surface in the interacting system suggests that, for a circular Fermi surface, Rashba coupling induces an effective triplite interaction. Consequently, we anticipate that superconductivity in this model is governed by an effective two-band Hamiltonian characterized by an intraband repulsive interaction and an interband attractive interaction. This finding provides a minimal theoretical framework for investigating non-Abelian topological superconductivity. We anticipate these insights will be relevant to experimental realizations using cold atoms and semiconductor-based two-dimensional electron gases.

Non-Abelian topological superconductivity, capable of hosting Majorana zero modes for quantum computing, may arise in two-dimensional superconducting systems with spin-polarized holes on honeycomb lattices. This paper demonstrates that the superconducting state in such systems is driven by an effective two-band mechanism, functioning as a sign-changing isotropic $s$-wave superconductor with an effective interband attraction. Specifically, when Rashba spin-orbit coupling and a Zeeman field eliminate the electron band and push hole bands away from the Fermi level, low-energy spin-polarized hole bands emerge. Subsequent supercooling leads to a second-order phase transition where the energy cost to create spin-polarized hole pairs is no longer infinite, establishing a finite energy gap. This indicates that the ground state is a two-band superconductor. Since the spin-polarized nature arises from the Zeeman field, spin-triplet components and an effective $\Delta_z$ pairing interaction coexist with spin-singlet $\Delta_{ab}$ interactions. This transition, occurring at doping levels of $x=p=0.17$ and in conditions characterized by magnetic fields above 35 T and temperatures well below the zero-field $T_c$, is manifested in the vortex lattice's compression modulus. Our analysis, grounded in the Eilenberger theory of vortex lattices, indicates that this event represents the anticipated 45-degree rotation of the square vortex lattice—a long-predicted phenomenon in $d$-wave superconductors occurring near a van Hove singularity. We have also characterized a preceding transition starting at higher temperatures, determined the activation energy associated with it, and linked this event to spin-density wave excitations. These observations offer a fresh viewpoint on the sequence of magnetic transitions in the underdoped region of LSCO and reinforce the connection between the vortex lattice and spins in $d$-wave superconductors. Ultimately, we argue that this novel transition serves as a critical endpoint for the "magnetic glass" phase recently reported in optimally doped LSCO. Recently reported magnetic transitions in the vortex state of optimally and underdoped LSCO have revealed an ordering temperature that varies with both doping and magnetic field. We propose a new scenario for these phenomena, positing that all observed magnetic transitions stem from a single underlying event: a 45-degree rotation of the vortex lattice. This rotation is triggered by the nesting of Fermi surfaces, a feature specific to the quasi-$d$-wave superconducting gap. Within this framework, we successfully reproduce the experimental data regarding the shift in magnetic transition temperatures with doping and the dependence of the transition entropy on the magnetic field in underdoped LSCO. Furthermore, we have formulated a scenario explaining the $\lambda$-shaped specific heat anomaly in optimally doped LSCO, an observation previously unexplained. We contend that the 45-degree lattice rotation constitutes a fundamental mesoscale phenomenon driving the macroscopic magnetic transitions. We attempted to synthesize a one-year ASM from a short-exposure, one-week observation dataset using three ML-based image processing techniques: dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise. Although ML inference yields less clarity than standard likelihood analysis, it generally enhanced the quality of the ASM. Notably, these algorithms successfully replicated the complex diffuse emission along the galactic plane from one-week data, effectively mimicking a ground truth (GT) derived from a full year of observations. These methods can be applied to any ASMs from mission-type gamma-ray telescopes. By combining multiple observations and leveraging ML, it should be possible to produce cleaner images than those from a single observation period. Furthermore, this approach could enable the detection of transient or variable sources by analyzing changes over time. Ultimately, this technique offers significant potential for single-telescope or collaborative multi-telescope single-epoch image reconstruction, where the counting statistics are insufficient for reliable source identification. This method is particularly valuable when applied to data with non-Poisson noise characteristics, such as data affected by channel dead times or background rejection cuts, where traditional analysis methods are not directly applicable. Additionally, the proposed method is computationally efficient.

In gamma-ray astronomy, single-telescope images are generated via likelihood methods, which are too time-consuming for gamma-ray transients. ML methods can reproduce these images quickly. Here, we apply such methods to one-week data from the wide-field, imaging, and image-reconstruction capable Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT). These methods successfully mimic the standard maximum-likelihood reconstruction, accurately reproducing both point sources and the galactic emission pattern. Consequently, ML techniques offer a way to identify transients that appear distinct when compared to the ground truth provided by a full year of observations.

Gamma-ray astronomy relies on image analysis to discover transients. However, because maximum-likelihood reconstruction is too computationally expensive to map entire skies, astronomers currently analyze only small regions. Our goal is to quickly identify transients using ML methods applied to ASM data. We tested three algorithms: k-means, FastICP, and GAN. The results demonstrate that these methods can mimic maximum-likelihood reconstruction and pinpoint point-like sources and galactic structures within minutes.

Each agent selects an action to maximize her own value, conditioned on the choices made by preceding agents. Our objective is to identify action sequences that achieve a total social welfare close to the optimal solution. We assume the ability to query the value $v_i(S)$ obtained by agent $i$ when acting after the set of agents $S$. We derive tight bounds on the social welfare achievable with a polynomial number of queries. While these general bounds indicate only a marginally sublinear approximation of optimal welfare, significantly better approximations emerge when valuations originate from specific combinatorial structures. For instance, when valuations correspond to bipartite matchings, directed graph arborescences, or Boolean satisfiability, query-efficient algorithms can produce near-optimal outcomes. In contrast, we demonstrate that linear query complexity yields at best constant-factor approximations for valuations based on weighted graph cut. Beyond providing unified bounds across various combinatorial optimization settings, our findings offer a fresh analytical lens for analyzing serial dictatorship-based algorithms prevalent in prior literature. Notably, existing analyses for these methods often rely on complex, value-oracle-independent probabilistic arguments to prove that allocated items form specific combinatorial objects. Our approach relies on query efficiency, recognizing that in practical applications, action values are frequently accessible either directly or through simple heuristics. A central component of our methodology is the introduction of combinatorial value amplification. We illustrate its utility by determining a finite query complexity for several established serial dictatorship algorithms reported in previous studies.

These techniques were subsequently applied to Pan-STARRS1 images of main belt asteroids ranging from 4 to 60 km in diameter. Since Johnston (2019) reports fewer than 10 known binaries in this size category with separations exceeding 10% of the primary's Hill radius, finding additional wide binaries is essential for determining the limits of binary stability and refining our understanding of asteroid masses. Our analysis involved two steps: first, comparing the major axis of an asteroid's elliptical PSF to its expected projected shape based on rotation, and second, examining local pixel-level residuals after deconvolving the PSF. ### Overview
Medical image analysis is essential for disease detection, diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring. Automated segmentation plays a critical role in this process by enabling the quantification of organ and tumor sizes. However, training robust and accurate segmentation models typically requires large volumes of labeled data, which is often difficult and expensive to obtain. Although self-supervised learning offers a potential solution by leveraging vast amounts of unlabeled data, it remains a significant hurdle in the medical imaging community. This paper presents a segmentation network trained using only unlabeled data through a two-stage process: first, training a network to reconstruct unlabeled images, and second, enhancing its segmentation capabilities through contrastive learning on unlabeled images without the need for ground

in Grounded Communication), a new task designed to investigate goal-oriented and grounded natural language interactions. To facilitate this study, we utilize Dungeons and Dragons (D&D) as our experimental platform; this role-playing game involves multiple player characters and a Dungeon Master (DM) who work together to reach shared objectives beneficial to the players. In this context, each player character represents a student with unique personas and capabilities, while the DM acts as the teacher, serving as the rule arbiter and guide responsible for helping students reach a global objective. We develop a theory-of-mind-inspired approach to train such a DM using reinforcement learning (RL). This methodology involves two key steps: first, the DM learns to anticipate player reactions to its statements by analyzing a dataset of D&D dialogue transcripts, and second, it employs these predictions as a reward function to evaluate how effectively its utterances guide players toward their goals. Both human and automated evaluations demonstrate that training a DM with RL to incorporate a theory-of-mind perspective significantly enhances the players' capacity to achieve goals grounded in their shared world. Additionally, we observe that this approach is particularly beneficial for less experienced D&D players and that the trained DM exhibits a preference for novice users. The code and datasets from this study are accessible via the following link: https://github.com/MingfengWA/G4C.

We investigate the utilization of large language models (LLMs) for natural language model evaluation. While recent research has applied LLMs to assess traditional encoder-decoder models through methods like self-assessment and teacher-assessment, these approaches often suffer when models generate extremely lengthy outputs, as seen in tasks such as professional translation, software testing, and abstractive summarization. Specifically, we find that when evaluating models on in-domain datasets, the assessment quality degrades as output length increases—a phenomenon we term the "long output effect." This issue is particularly pronounced when using few-shot prompting schemes to enhance LLM performance without access to external datasets. We examine the underlying causes of this problem and propose two straightforward strategies to mitigate the long output effect, a challenge that is currently under-examined in contemporary research. We provide a comprehensive experimental analysis comparing these methods against two established baseline approaches across three distinct datasets. Our findings indicate that while the long output effect represents a significant constraint in the evaluation of long-generated text, our proposed techniques can effectively address this issue. We have open-sourced all code and datasets used in this study at https://github.com/XuandLing/Evaluation-of-LLMs.

The observation that new information constantly replaces old within the brain has long fueled theories of human memory as a system of constantly updating "copies." While largely unexplored in current AI, this paper introduces a model where a Transformer generates a summary of its prior outputs to inform subsequent predictions. We show that this mechanism not only facilitates the handling of unlimited context but also induces a sentence-representation update rule that mirrors human memory physiology. By leveraging this rule, we achieve the retrieval and activation of older information using only a linear layer, thereby eliminating the need for dense storage. This approach leads to a new model of hierarchical memory with energetic optimization properties, offering a framework for retrieving and activating ancient experiences through a local activation rule similar to Hebbian learning. Such a system enables the perception of meaning in life and the recognition of evolutionary patterns, providing a model of memory that balances metabolic efficiency with expressive fidelity to the past. Code is available at https://github.com/maxwj24/Hierarchical_Memory.

Recent research categorizes the topology and geometry of knotted proteins by examining the distribution of their planar projections through topological entities known as knotoids. We adopt a similar analytical framework by developing a topologically grounded statistical metric to compare knotoid distributions among proteins sharing the same topology. Our method identifies geometric variations between trefoil proteins by quantifying their entanglement and by examining turns in their tangent vectors, an approach consistent with previous topological studies. By combining these metrics, we create a metric space that effectively separates the two trefoil variants. Furthermore, analyzing the geodesics within this space reveals that distribution differences arise from a combination of re-entry frequency and pitch. This study introduces knotoids as a robust tool for investigating the topology and geometry of proteins, nucleic acids, and other biological polymers. We suggest extending this method to explore geometric aspects in other knotted structures, such as gas-phase or liquid-crystalline nucleic acid knots, as well as in nature-like entangled objects like sea pens and marine worms. Finally, we propose utilizing this approach for functional comparisons in proteomics. We align with prior work [Melhuish et al, arXiv:1909.01004] by asserting that open curve theory offers a robust framework for classifying and comparing the topology and geometry of protein knots and other closed or open polymers. Such analysis is crucial not only for understanding the formation, diversity, and stability of natural protein knots but also for the topological design of synthetic polymers with potential applications in drug delivery, gene therapy, and gene expression.

==Introduction==

Counterfactual data enables models to internalize the structural relationships between inputs and outputs, fostering improved robustness and generalization. Despite these advantages, acquiring high-quality counterfactual datasets is difficult due to the scarcity of human-labeled examples and the high cost of expanding into new perturbation spaces. This post introduces a system for generating data with a specific cause-and-effect structure and discusses its impact on model generalization and robustness.

===Background===

Counterfactual reasoning involves making minimal alterations to a data point $(x,y)$ to create a new instance $(x',y)$ that remains semantically valid (General et al., 2017). For instance, changing the tense of a sentence ("The cat chased the rat" $\rightarrow$ "The cat was chasing the rat") or modifying the sentiment of a review ("The pizza was delicious" $\rightarrow$ "The pizza was not delicious") serves as a counterfactual transformation.

Although recent work demonstrates that this data helps models understand input-output structures and enhances robustness (Shen et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021), two primary hurdles remain:

1.  **Scale and Diversity:** Current publicly available counterfactual datasets are restricted to a few perturbation types, such as synonyms (Hai et al., 2020) or insertions/delet

Federated Learning provides a privacy-preserving method to train machine learning models across distributed data sources. However, it lacks the capability to create personalized models for specific users. To overcome this limitation, we introduce FedHealth, which integrates a privacy-preserving transfer learning approach with federated learning for wearable activity classification. FedHealth enables the development of highly accurate, user-specific activity classifiers by leveraging diverse data sourced from multiple apps and devices. The framework's efficacy has been demonstrated in two distinct settings: (1) predicting specific activities using time-series data with high class imbalance, and (2) binary disease detection based on scalar data that varies significantly between individuals. Experimental findings show that FedHealth yields a 5.3% improvement in accuracy compared to centrally trained baselines and supports multi-task scenarios by maintaining performance across different target domains. In essence, FedHealth advances machine learning for distributed data by facilitating both customized models and enhanced accuracy.

We present a unified approach combining FL with transfer learning to develop a framework for training both machine and deep learning models on data from wearable devices. Given the scarcity—or potential absence—of stable de Sitter vacua, dark energy in string theory is presumed to manifest as a quintessence field undergoing slow roll. As this field evolves, a tower of massive states will generically become lighter, initiating a catastrophic phase transition in low-energy cosmological dynamics within at most a few hundred Hubble times. venshtein introduced the sequence reconstruction problem, which examines a scenario where an identical sequence from a specific set is sent through several channels, with the decoder observing the resulting distinct outputs. Assuming the transmitted sequence lies at a distance $d$ from a code and that each channel introduces no more than $r$ errors, the goal is to determine the minimum number of channels necessary to uniquely recover the original sequence. This number must exceed the maximum overlap between two metric balls of radius $r$, provided their centers are separated by at least distance $d$. This paper investigates the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations using Hamming distance. Within this framework, we define a Cayley graph and calculate the precise value of the largest intersection of two metric balls under Hamming distance for the cases where $r=4$ and $d\geqslant 5$, as well as when $d=2r$. These findings enable us to refine lower bounds on the number of channel-specific permutations required to guarantee error-correctable transmission of any permutation of length $n$. Additionally, we derive an upper bound on the count of straight permutations that can be reconstructed from four noisy outputs. To achieve this, we develop a novel method for analyzing permutations based on their cycle structures. \medskip

We begin by outlining the fundamental characteristics of the classic Kermack-McKendrick models before exploring their generalizations and applications to contact networks, viral co-circulation, epidemic curve trajectories, probability distributions, and passage times required to define compartments in these models. Collectively, these examples underscore that a system of differential equations designed for a specific epidemiological challenge relies fundamentally on the epidemiological, medical, and biological context driving its formulation and analysis. Merely fitting differential models to data without considering biological feasibility may yield statistically significant results but will ultimately fail to offer actionable insights for managing, mitigating, or controlling the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. Following the introduction, a literature review, and a section on the formation and analysis of differential and integral models, the discussion focuses on net reproduction rates, epidemic curves, viral co-circulation, epidemic generation times, and their implications for mitigating the outbreak. We conclude by exploring potential model applications for resuming inter- and intra-country travel, reopening economies, and developing vaccines. In the final section, we present an overview of where the fight against the virus currently stands and where the research community hopes to gain deeper insights into epidemic dynamics and the virus itself through mathematical modeling. This study does not claim to be exhaustive; rather, it aims to bring researchers, including epidemiologists, epidemiological modelers, epidemiological model users, epidemiological model critics, epidemiological policymakers, and the general public, closer to understanding the vital role mathematical modeling plays in analyzing and forming opinions on the virus, its effects, transmission dynamics, transmission routes, transmission patterns, transmission strategies, and more. Additionally, we emphasize how these models can inform decisions on reopening economies and schools, as well as establishing vaccination thresholds. The associated materials can be accessed at: http://arizona.edu/~mmabbed/Models-and-the-SARS-CoV-2-Epidemic.pdf. We declare no conflicts of interest.

While natural language processing techniques can locate acronyms, they often fail to provide a comprehensive list of their meanings. Our methodology employs a multi-task learning framework to simultaneously train disjoint task-specific models for discrete sets of domains. Each domain utilizes features tailored to its unique characteristics, and a transfer learning approach facilitates the transfer of knowledge between these specialized models.

Our method utilizes a multi-task learning approach with a novel multi-layer attention mechanism. This implementation allows for the integration of domain-specific features with knowledge transfer between related fields, ensuring robust performance across diverse contexts.

Specifically, we analyze how, under appropriate dark-state conditions, the interaction between spin-exchange collisions and photoassociation facilitates the stable formation of atom-molecule pairs from three initial spin-zero atoms. This mechanism, involving two distinct two-body interactions, can be conceptually understood as an effective three-body recombination. We explore the respective influences of photoassociation and initial magnetization in the "resonant" scenario where the dark-state condition is perfectly met. Additionally, we investigate the "non-resonant" regime, where this condition is either approximately fulfilled (the adiabatic case) or not met at all. In the adiabatic scenario, we develop an effective non-linear Schrodinger equation for the condensate wavefunction, based on two effective masses and potential derived through an adiabatic approximation, to analyze the dynamics of coherent atom-molecule formation. Furthishly, we propose a non-resonant atom-molecule condensate laser, which we demonstrate can achieve stable atom-molecule pair condensation even when the dark-state condition is significantly violated. This approach requires only weakly magnetized and cool spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensates, making it practically feasible in current experiments. The observed dynamics could potentially enhance the stability of conventional photoassociation processes. Our proposal of coherent atom-molecule pairing condensation offers multiple potential applications, including the interaction between an atom and a molecule, sensor technology, and as a platform for examining a few-body version of the Haldane-Shastry model. Consequently, this research could advance the few-body physics of atom-molecules, particularly diatomic molecules.

Unlike previous approaches, our system treats a 20-base-pair PCR primer pair not as a definition for a single object, but as a distinct storage partition managed independently with its own indexing structure. We observe that while the total number of compatible primer pairs is constrained, the internal address space within each partition is virtually limitless. By exploiting the flexibility of this address space, we enable advanced storage semantics, including hierarchical organization and robust, efficient data update mechanisms. Additionally, to maximize the potential of PCR's prefix-based addressing, we developed a method to convert any arbitrary indexing scheme into a PCR-compatible format. This allows primers to be dynamically extended to include specific index segments, thereby narrowing the reaction scope to precisely retrieve individual objects (such as files or directories) within a partition. Our wet lab validation confirms the feasibility of this approach and demonstrates a 140-fold reduction in sequencing costs when retrieving smaller objects from a partition. We estimate that the potential sequencing economy of using this update strategy compared to traditional storage methods exceeds four orders of magnitude. Since the primary constraints of DNA storage are sequence length and PCR compatibility, and since our method requires no increase in length or additional primers, it can be integrated into any existing DNA-storage framework to significantly enhance functionality. The GitHub repository for our simulation and optimization tools is available at https://github.com/AlonLinnainmaa/dna_hierarchy.

This design supports various data update operations, such as replacing an object with a new version, merging two objects, or combining multiple versions. To mitigate the high per-base synthesis cost of DNA, we recommend utilizing wildcards in the extended portions of the updated primers.

Although recent investigations have uncovered the existence and characteristics of topological nodal lines, significant challenges remain regarding their creation, observation, and manipulation. This review examines the recent advances and diverse examples of topological nodal lines within artificial structures, including photonic and phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits. By summarizing these developments, the review provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of research on topological nodal lines in artificial materials.

Recent studies have demonstrated that nodal lines can exhibit topological features, such as the $\mathbb{Z}$ index and a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ index, leading to the emergence of additional topological invariants like the link number and Hopf invariant. This review provides a pedagogical explanation of topological nodal lines, discussing how they can be manipulated to create "higher-order" topological phases through the stacking of multiple nodal lines.

While it enhances traditional optimization methods by enabling adjustment to new scenes or sensors without retraining, it also allows for the resolution of telescopic issues using only corrupted images as training data. However, current deep differentiable renderers, such as Neural Radiance Fields (NRF), face a key limitation: they typically lack fine high-frequency details, a deficit that becomes critical in inverse problem applications. To address this, we introduce a novel, simple, and efficient differentiable renderer based on the rendering framework first proposed by Kautz et al. This approach learns separate high- and low-frequency components, with the method's performance hinging primarily on the quality of the high-frequency term. We evaluate the technique on both synthetic and real datasets, including images captured by a mobile device and a NR5 hand-held nanosecond white LED. The results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art differentiable rendering quality. Furthermore, we illustrate how our method can be leveraged to solve various inverse problems, including shape reconstruction from a single RGB image (without depth supervision), depth maps, color images, and hybrid sensors that combine only corrupted data. In all scenarios, our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions. For instance, in single-image shape reconstruction, our method requires approximately 10 times less memory, renders 3 to 4 times faster, and delivers 3 times better gradient metrics. Similarly, in depth map reconstruction, our method is roughly 10 times more memory-efficient, renders 4 to 5 times faster, and achieves 3 times superior gradient quality compared to current state-of-the-art solutions. These advantages stem from the simplicity of our rendering formulation. Consequently, our method is well-suited for inverse problem solving, offering significant improvements in memory efficiency, rendering speed, and more than a tenfold increase in usable memory—amounting to approximately 100 times less memory than required by current state-of-the-art techniques. In contrast to approaches relying on external priors, our method stands alone as the first capable of solving all examined inverse problems solely through corrupted images. Additionally, our method renders 4 to 5 times faster than recent memory-efficient renderers like MipSDF. Source code is available at https://github.com/david-wang-99/HiLoRS. We hope our method will inspire future research in both differentiable rendering and image-based inverse problems.

Regarding the neutron skin of $^{208}$Pb, the calculated root mean square radius for the point neutron density distribution is 0.075 fm. This is derived from the ratio of the neutron matter radius to the proton matter radius being 0.99575. It is important to note that the formula used in this study was not applied to other heavy nuclei because it yields a neutron skin thickness that is too small for them. The discrepancy in neutron skin thickness between non-relativistic and relativistic mean field theories arises from the shift in the single-nucleon $s$-wave bound state under the influence of the vector potential. Human-Promoted Video Generation transforms ordinary clips into emotionally resonant content by dynamically aligning visuals, captions, and voiceovers to tell a targeted story. Although widespread in the streaming era, comprehensive automatic generation in this sphere remains nascent, with existing work primarily focusing on backend visual editing. To address the lack of research on the full pipeline, we introduce a comprehensive framework encompassing three core stages: content-aware audio generation, semantic-aware captioning, and an integrated framework for the complete generative process. This work represents the first effort to systematically address human-promoted video generation across its entire spectrum.
Human-Promoted Video Generation produces emotionally engaging content by dynamically aligning visuals, captions, and voiceovers for specific audiences. Despite its prevalence in the video streaming era, rigorous automatic generation research remains in its infancy, with current efforts largely limited to the visual editing component. Conscientious of the lack of study on the complete pipeline, we propose a framework addressing the full human-promoted video generation process, including content-aware audio generation, semantic-aware captioning, and a unified integrated system. This paper pioneers comprehensive research into this domain.

Text attacks that rely on heuristic defenses, such as those based on input perturbation, often suffer from low attack strength and poor generalization. Our comprehensive empirical study demonstrates that these characterizations significantly improve the power and generalization of text-based attacks, yielding a 5.6% average increase in attack success rate (ASR) across various defense mechanisms and a 25% boost in ASR on unlabeled test images. This study examines the dispersion of a population of fractional Brownian walkers, which exhibit long-time correlations and possess time-dependent, heterogeneous diffusivity. The goal is to determine the resulting diffusion equation and verify it through numerical simulations. The findings reveal that the population consists of two distinct groups: fast walkers with high diffusivity that quickly spread, and slow walkers with low diffusivity that gradually join the moving crowd. Consequently, the root mean square displacement grows faster than linearly during the intermediate period before ultimately returning to linear growth in the long-term limit. This behavior is attributed to the immediate contribution of the fast walkers to the crowd's expansion, whereas the slow walkers reduce the dispersion in the long-term regime compared to single-agent diffusers. The simulated concentration profiles align well with the analytically derived solutions. This model is applicable to various scenarios involving individual heterogeneity and correlations, such as the spread of diseases, particle deposition, and crowd dynamics. Furthermore, the approach may be extended to describe non-Gaussian spreading in other contexts, including the lipid diffusion required for virus entry into cells and active particle diffusion within a lipid membrane.
In this work, we examine a model of an expanding population composed of fractional Brownian walkers, which are agents following a Hamiltonian with time-correlated noise and time-dependent mass. This framework is relevant to systems like granular materials, expanding glasses, and swarms of biological cells, often leading to nonlinear diffusion equations and varying mass distributions. We explore the model's behavior in both infinite and bounded domains with reflective boundaries across different dimensions. While the center of mass always follows linear diffusion, the mass distribution can become highly non-uniform due to dimension-dependent freezing or phase separation at the center, potentially forming a "black hole." In finite dimensions, the profile converges to a uniform density at the center (infinite diffusivity) with all mass at the center of expansion in the long-term limit; this is not the case in fractional dimensions. The model can also be adapted for walkers with time-dependent interaction strengths, where the weighting exponent matches the Hurst exponent of the fractional Brownian noise. This generalized model offers insights into self-propelled walkers, many-body problems, and other systems with embedded correlations and heterogeneity, potentially offering a framework to map those models onto simpler non-interacting walkers with uniform masses.

In battery electric vehicles (BEVs), the drive motor and power electronics (PE) are typically housed within the same enclosure, creating a shared thermal environment that complicates the prediction of component temperatures. While machine learning (ML) models can aid thermal management by leveraging the interdependency of temperatures, the scarcity of data during vehicle development constrains model training. Our study develops a ML solution based on conditional generative adversarial networks (CGGANs) to accurately estimate the motor temperature given the sensor readings excluding the motor's internal temperature. Similarly, the PE temperature can be reconstructed using all other available sensor data. Although trained on data from a single stationary test bench, the model demonstrates reconstruction accuracy comparable to physical measurements. By enabling the estimation of component temperatures from existing sensor configurations, this approach allows for the improvement of component lifespans or the allocation of measurement budgets to the most critical components when sensor counts are limited. Although evaluated in a specific context, the methodology is broadly applicable to any system governed by coupled thermal phenomena.

Although deep reinforcement learning has shown promising results in controlled environments, it struggles to generalize to new situations and tasks, often requiring extensive interaction. We present Lifelong Exploration with Representational Desires (LLEX), which allows a single policy to master multiple tasks while continuously learning from unstructured interactions with an environment. By integrating generative exploration with recurrent attention mechanisms, LLEX teaches the policy to seek out informative states and actions that yield novel experiences. We show that LLEX facilitates the acquisition of useful priors, allowing a neural network to match or exceed state-of-the-art performance on complex robotic tasks that would otherwise be difficult to train. Experimental results indicate that LLEX learns a robotic insertion task 5x faster than existing methods and achieves a 25% higher success rate on a challenging dynamic human-robot interaction problem.*Our code and datasets can be accessed here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3zIb-1eU76I.

This study introduces an algorithm for identifying negative selection rules that explain why certain word sequences are chosen as translations for specific target words. Such rules function as pattern-matching mechanisms that guide machine translation. We evaluate the algorithm's performance using a process that involves two steps: first, measuring the coverage of rules derived from a source corpus, and second, assessing their plausibility using a parallel corpus. The algorithm operates by selecting rules that maximize a score representing the balance between their coverage and plausibility. Additionally, we examine how selected rules vary according to source language characteristics and their utility in translating out-of-vocabulary words.

This study examines a two-trophic ecosystem involving two predator species that compete for a shared prey resource, incorporating explicit interference competition. Through a linear stability analysis of the coexistence equilibrium, specific ecosystems identified as prone to regime shifts are characterized. The relative strength of this competition is modeled as a parameter; in selected systems, increasing it triggers a Hopf bifurcation, causing the system to oscillate and ultimately undergo a collapse in biometric volume. The competition coefficient is constructed using functional response terms, with the Type-II response being the most prevalent in nature. Both analytical findings and numerical simulations using a system of ordinary differential equations confirm that the type of interference competition among predators significantly influences regime shifts and their associated dynamics. Furthermore, when predator population growth follows a logistic pattern, different response types—Type-II, Type-III, and Type-IV—are explored. The predominant Type-II functional response is found to accelerate regime shifts. Additionally, the parameter space is divided into distinct regions separated by a separatrix. Introducing asymmetric interference competition helps differentiate between alternative stable states and avoids undesirable oscillatory behavior. Finally, the impact of delayed response times to changes in prey density is simulated using a simulating delay term within the interference competition function. This model demonstrates that higher delays increase the likelihood of a predator collapse. Consequently, managing delayed interference competition among top predators may help prevent sudden shifts to alternative stable states or population collapses. These state shifts can be further exacerbated by stochastic environmental fluctuations and external human activities. This model offers a deeper understanding of predator competition dynamics and their contribution to regime shifts within ecological systems. In conclusion, the proposed model contributes to the theoretical framework of non-equilibrium population dynamics, particularly regarding predator competition and regime shifts, and holds potential utility in predicting and controlling pest outbreaks in agricultural and forested areas. We introduce a new formal model that encapsulates the semantics of programs executing under such protocols. Leveraging this model, we developed a static analysis technique to identify specific sequences of memory instructions that result in semantic discrepancies compared to reference sequential executions. By employing a Jackiw-Kerman style Hartree-type two-body trial wavefunction, we derive an effective semiclassical Hamiltonian. Numerical findings demonstrate that quantum effects can indeed generate chaos within the non-chaotic regions of the classical H\'enon-Heiles system. Furthermore, as the quantum number $N$ rises, the spectral spacing $\Delta E$ diminishes, eventually reaching the classical energy values of the non-chaotic H\'enon-Heiles system in the large $N$ limit. Additionally, by analyzing the Lyapunov exponent $\lambda$, the entropy $K$ derived from the slope of the three-dimensional Wigner distribution, and the participation ratio $R$, we determine the fractional entropy $f = \frac{K+1}{2}$ to characterize the nature of chaos in this framework. We observe that $f$ fluctuates in the low $N$ regime but converges to $\frac{1}{2}$ in the large $N$ limit, signaling a transition from quantum chaos to classical chaos. Notably, the choice of scaling for the expectation value of the square radius $\langle r^2 \rangle$ critically influences the behavior of $R$ and, consequently, the dynamics of $f$. Finally, by plotting the phase space of quasiclassical probability density in the $(q_1,p_1)$ plane, we further illustrate the emergence of chaos in the non-chaotic areas of the classical H\'enon-Heiles system. This study provides additional support for the quasiclassical characterization of chaos and underscores the potential of the $f$-characterized fractional entropy for classifying quantum chaos in systems with separable variables. We conclude that the non-chaotic domains of the classical H\'enon-Heiles system correspond to the low $N$ regime of the quantum system, whereas the chaotic domains of the classical system align with the large $N$ limit of the quantum system. The term "classical chaos" in this context refers to a state where phase space is no longer uniformly populated.

The primary objective of this article is to present a Content Addressable Parallel Processor (CAPP) designed for real-time applications and implemented on an FPGA. Specifically, we investigated the physical characteristics of the two most luminous starbursts, eClGordo 1a and eClGordo 2a, including their combined system (referred to as eClGordo 1&2). Our analysis addresses the cluster's gravitational potential, gas distribution, and the verification of the optical/IR alignment between eClGordo 1&2. These three eClGordo targets represent the most massive and luminous star-forming galaxies within the cluster. Notably, eClGordo 1&2 are nearly aligned and almost symmetrically positioned relative to the mass center of eClGordo. This symmetric configuration, along with a supersonic shock detected behind eClGordo 1&2 via sub-millimeter observations, strongly suggests that the enhanced star formation activity in eClGordo 1&2 is driven by the accretion of cold gas triggered by the shock. Based on this scenario, we constructed simulation models for these galaxy clusters. We successfully reproduced the global optical properties of eClGordo, as well as the optical characteristics of its member galaxies, including the extended dust component observed in eClGordo 1&2. Our approach not only accurately explains the observed optical properties of the system but also correctly predicts the sub-millimeter emission from the hot gas and dust in these $z=0.87$ galaxy clusters. However, we note that the specific formation mechanism of the supersonic shock behind eClGordo 1&2 remains unexplained by both our model and current theoretical frameworks. Based on the constraints imposed by these observations, we established criteria for selecting plausible dynamical scenarios for massive galaxy cluster formations. These criteria will serve as a foundation for developing more comprehensive multi-scale models that explicitly incorporate sub-grid physics governing small-scale phenomena. Finally, we concluded that the formal uncertainty in the total mass of eClGordo amounts to approximately 10%. The findings presented in this paper will be extended in future work to include additional observational data obtained from newly constructed instruments. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a neurosymbolic approach that leverages weak supervision from a static program analyzer. This method enables a deep generative model to symbolically identify long-distance semantic relationships within already generated code by invoking static-analysis tools. During training, the model learns to generate programs conditioned on these computed relationships. We demonstrate this technique on the task of generating full Java methods given the surrounding class context. Experimental results indicate that our approach significantly outperforms both leading transformer models and architectures explicitly designed to learn program semantics, achieving superior performance in both syntactic accuracy and the elimination of basic semantic errors. Consequently, we can now generate methods that adhere more closely to the semantics of their parent class. We further illustrate how this technique is applicable to program completion and debugging. The source code for our implementation is available open-source at https://github.com/google/deepmind-fair_models/tree/public/symbolic-static-analysis-for-neural-code-generation.

To address the challenge of generating program statements with correct inter-statement dependencies, we utilize program-analysis tools such as linters and static analyzers. These tools assist in learning how generated code should function by providing hints about common coding errors and semantic issues, as well as offering insights into program structure. We show that models trained with this method substantially outperform recent state-of-the-art approaches designed to learn program semantics, including CodeBERT, CM3, and Programmatic Neural Networks (PNNs).

Recent advancements in program synthesis have enabled the generation of individual statements or simple expressions with high accuracy, yet these models often fail to produce multi-statement programs or longer sequences of statements correctly. This failure stems from the absence of programs with appropriate context from current training datasets. We propose a solution where a model is trained to predict the outputs of a static-program-analysis tool applied to the code it generates. This allows the model to learn both semantic constraints and the internal mapping between program syntax and semantics from datasets lacking such information. We implement this by training a model to output a vector embedding of the static analysis results for its generated code, utilizing an attention mechanism to integrate this information when producing the final code. This framework is demonstrated on two tasks: generating full methods from class-level context and synthesizing C statements. In both cases, our model markedly surpasses recent state-of-the-art systems and various baselines.

Data from our records, alongside observations from GOES 11 and SOHO satellites, indicate that electrons and protons—potential byproducts of neutron decay—were present. While solar neutron decay protons (sndp) were previously detected aboard the ISEE3 satellite on June 3, 1982, and by ground-level instruments in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19, 1989, this marks the second instance of such evidence being recorded directly on Earth's surface. Our data support the notion of neutron production occurring high within the atmosphere, rather than neutrons penetrating through it. However, attributing neutron-generated electrons and sndp exclusively to a specific flare interaction remains challenging. Although our findings contradict the idea that snds are merely protons formed by neutron decay, they align perfectly with our proposal that these particles resulted from the direct impact of a neutron pulse. This event offers significant value for comprehending the mechanisms behind solar neutron pulses (sndp) and their associated byproducts. Furthermore, the findings support the notion that the traditional three-component model of solar particle events (SPEs)—comprising electrons, protons, and neutrons—might be inaccurate. Instead, at very high energies, solar particle events might consist of only two components: electrons and protons. Additionally, the paper addresses the longstanding challenge of explaining how neutrons can penetrate the Earth's atmosphere given its properties. Finally, the term "solar neutron pulse" is defined for the first time, with a recommendation that this new terminology be adopted in future research. The appendix provides the mathematical foundation for our conclusions regarding the atmosphere's opacity to neutrons and the multi-component nature of solar neutron pulses.

This phenomenon has triggered multiple real-world crises, including election interference and pandemic dissemination. Although detection models exist, they struggle to identify deceptive content related to new events because of shifts in language and context. Consequently, detectors must navigate semantic shifts across contexts and lexical changes when encountering unseen event domains.

### Conclusion

Lesions resulting from LITT are a recent development in epilepsy treatment, restricting the amount of available data for developing effective litten (LITT) segmentation models due to a lack of large-scale datasets. This study introduces a data augmentation framework (PAVAE) tailored for litten segmentation, addressing the challenge of limited and varied training data. Our approach involves two sequential networks: a mask synthesis network and a mask-guided litten synthesis network. By incorporating two specialized embedding modules—the mask embedding block (MEB) and condition embedding block (CEB)—we achieved high-quality data augmentation, resulting in substantial improvements for downstream segmentation models. Specifically, a U-Net model trained on a mixture of raw and synthetic data attained superior performance on three distinct validation sets relative to models trained solely on raw data. It is important to note that our framework is designed exclusively for data augmentation and has not been evaluated against other advanced data augmentation techniques. Future enhancements could include integrating other sophisticated segmentation architectures for more accurate synthesis or adopting a joint learning strategy for simultaneous mask and lesion synthesis.

PD is a neurodegenerative condition characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, which disrupts the normal dynamics of the basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex circuit. Furthermore, the approach is applicable to other computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can be used to fit multi-scale brain circuit models.

Parkinson's Disease is a prevalent global condition affecting over 10 million individuals, with no current cure available. Caused by the death of dopamine-producing neurons in the brain, the disease leads to severe motor and non-motor impairments. Although various treatments exist, they offer only partial relief and do not halt progression. While the link between neuron loss and disease symptoms is clear, many aspects of how the disease develops remain unknown, necessitating further research. We argue that the most effective strategy to address these gaps involves a new class of computational models of the brain that integrate data from animal studies. This paper details a significant challenge faced by such models: the difficulty of simultaneously fitting data from three papers, which reported electrophysiological recordings from seven different brain regions in marmoset monkeys, both in healthy and parkinsonian states. We show that a computational model of the Parkinson's disease basal ganglia, combined with an additional mechanism, can accurately reproduce electrophysiological data from these studies. These findings underscore the viability of computational models in exploring the molecular origins of brain disorders and developing strategies to treat them.

Current approaches typically rely on sensor arrays or in-vehicle cameras to forecast weather, yet these methods incur incremental costs and offer limited scope. To guarantee the uninterrupted operation of all transportation services regardless of conditions, a robust detection system capable of classifying weather in the wild is essential. However, solving this problem is challenging due to the diverse nature of weather conditions and the lack of distinctive features across different scenarios. Existing solutions are often scene-specific and restricted to classifying only two weather categories. This paper introduces a novel open-source dataset named RFS, comprising images of three weather classes: rain, snow, and fog. Additionally, a new algorithm is proposed that employs super-pixel delimiting masks for data augmentation, achieving reasonable performance across ten Convolutional Neural Network architectures. Experimental results indicate that the new algorithm attains state-of-the-art status. On a difficult validation set featuring rain and fog, the algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods by margins of 9.6%, 8.4%, and 6.8% in terms of Accuracy, Recall, and F1-Score, respectively. This approach is appealing because it relies on fundamental dynamics, thereby circumventing the invalid assumptions found in mass-flux convection schemes at current resolutions. Nevertheless, the optimal closure mechanisms for each fluid—distinguishing between rising thermals, sinking sinks, and the ambient fluid—and the minimal grid resolution required for correct fluid behavior remain unclear. This study investigates these uncertainties using a straightforward dry convection model. We find that correctly representing the spectrum of fluid scales is crucial for accurately modeling atmospheric convection. Specifically, when the dissipation scale is expressed relative to the boundary layer depth, nine distinct fluid scales are necessary to resolve a 1 km grid to within a factor of two. Given the cubic relationship between resolution and the number of required fluids, achieving accurate 1 km convective modeling would necessitate approximately 40 times more computational resources than current schemes. However, if an approximate distribution of scales is employed, five fluids would suffice to achieve comparable accuracy at the current 27 km resolution, offering a promising pathway to make sub-50 km resolution convective modeling feasible in regional or global simulations. Furthermore, the derived approximate scale distribution can be understood through the framework of self-gravitating fluids.
Recently, multi-fluid models have been proposed to more accurately represent convecting atmospheres by avoiding the broken laws inherent in subgrid convection parametrizations. This method models the atmosphere by applying average conservation laws to distinct fluids, such as the bulk fluid, actively rising thermals, and actively sinking plumes. While this approach is advantageous for its reliance on fundamental physics, making it suitable for  climate models at approximately 1 km resolution, several unaddressed challenges remain. This paper examines the optimal set of fluids and the resolution needs for their closure. By systematically varying the number of fluids and grid spacing in a simplified dry thermal boundary layer model, we derive the necessary conditions for the study. Our results indicate that, for a given resolution, using six fluids without an ambient fluid layer introduces an error no greater than 30% in the boundary layer height. Conversely, to accurately predict the scale distribution (within a factor of 2), one would need roughly 40 fluids. This approach establishes the optical tomogram as a fundamental physical quantity capable of exhibiting its own distinct nonclassical features.

Reconstructing the phase-space representation of continuous-variable quantum states, particularly the Wigner function, from optical tomograms is hindered by significant difficulties. Specifically, the optical tomograms of squeezed states reveal that their nonclassical characteristics are inherent to the tomograms themselves and even concentrate in regions of negative values within the Wigner function. We propose that certain local structures in the optical tomograms, identifiable as "optical squeezings," serve as direct indicators of entanglement and certain types of quantum synchronization in multi-mode systems. Moreover, the degree of these optical entanglement and synchronization can be quantified semi-quantitatively or qualitatively through specific optical squeezing structures. The formation and evolution of these entanglement and synchronization phenomena are driven by the same mechanisms that generate the optical squeezing structures. By utilizing these structures, one can not only detect but also distinguish different forms and types of continuous-variable quantum entanglement and synchronization. Consequently, the complex task of reconstructing the global Wigner function can be bypassed in favor of a more accessible analysis of the optical tomograms for state reconstruction.

We show that entanglement in continuous-variable quantum systems can be identified through the optical tomograms of divided light fields, specifically via the emergence of dark strips. This reveals an distinct entanglement structure and its development within the optical tomographic representation of continuous-variable light states.

Abstract
To evaluate the control options available to farmers, researchers commonly assess the stochastic efficiency of net returns, often utilizing random effects models or simulations. These methods rely on large datasets, a condition rarely met in experimental field settings. Additionally, the standard analysis fails to account for disease pressure; while control costs are fixed, damage costs are not. This research offers a solution that leverages simulations to address data limitations while integrating disease pressure analysis using a quantile regression model. The findings from a case study on strawberry disease management in Florida demonstrate that although stochastic efficiency and effect estimates align with existing literature, the proposed method significantly improves statistical power. Moreover, the study highlights the non-linear nature of the relationship between disease pressure, pressure margins, and profitability.
To determine the best disease management tactics for strawberry farmers, researchers examine the impact of various control methods on plant damage and net returns. This analysis typically evaluates the stochastic efficiency of net returns, often employing general linear models or similar statistical approaches. However, these methods demand large datasets, which is challenging in disease field experiments due to the limited number of replication trials. Moreover, standard analyses overlook the role of disease pressure. Since control costs are constant while damage costs vary, understanding how pressure affects profitability is crucial. This study introduces a method that utilizes simulations to solve data limitations and incorporates disease pressure analysis using a quantile regression model. The results from a case study on strawberry disease management in Florida confirm that the proposed approach significantly boosts statistical power while aligning with traditional effect estimates and stochastic efficiency findings from previous studies. Additionally, the study underscores the non-linear relationship between disease pressure, pressure margins, and profitability.

However, when the user performs rapid head turns, the transition from CFV to full 360-degree content generates a significant visual discrepancy known as peripheral distortion. This paper evaluates the feasibility of conducting a sensitive test of the Weak Equivalence Principle (WEP) using data from the TEST卫星 mission. The TEST卫星 is an upcoming satellite equipped with a precision accelerometry instrument specifically designed to minimize systematic errors and to test the WEP with a sensitivity approximately ten times greater than the recently published MICROSCOPE experiment's constraint. This document details the construction of the TEST卫星 and its instruments, outlining the optimal orbital parameters and operational strategies required to maximize sensitivity to a potential WEP violation. Such a test would significantly constrain specific theoretical extensions of general relativity, which are currently the primary candidates for formulating a quantum theory of gravity. The findings presented in this document will guide the operation of the TEST卫星, which is scheduled for construction to follow the MICROSCOPE mission in 2026, with a planned launch in 2027.

Traditionally, this process requires access to both the training data and the teacher's internal parameters, a setup often impractical in real-world scenarios due to storage constraints or privacy concerns. To address this, we introduce Decision-Based Black-Box (DB3) knowledge distillation, which trains a student model using a black-box teacher that reveals only class labels instead of softmax probabilities. Our approach first addresses cases where training data is available: we calculate a sample's robustness against the teacher by measuring how softmax scores distribute across classes as decision-based queries (class labels) are applied, then use this sensitivity as a proxy for the teacher's softmax output in standard KD. This query network, trained on data-free decision queries (class labels), infers the teacher's softmax outputs based on the same robustness analysis used when training data exists, enabling complete data-free DB3 knowledge distillation. Experiments on ImageNet demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of our methods. Specifically, when training data is available, our approach achieves a 96% accuracy student model by distilling from a teacher with 5% accuracy using a Fano-Moreno plot loss function. When training data is absent, our extension successfully trains a 20% accurate student by querying a 76.32% accurate teacher. Across various configurations, our methods significantly outperform existing black-box and decision-based techniques. The code for DB3 is available at https://github.com/Zeyu-Liu/DB3.
