The vast diversity of life has resulted in a wide array of locomotive designs and methods, with various creatures utilizing legs, wings, fins, and other mechanisms to traverse their environments. This report defines the movement of general biological species as biolocomotion and introduces a computational method to identify it within raw video footage. Crucially, the motion of biological entities navigating an environment can be modeled as a superposition of overall positional advancement and an asymmetric oscillatory pattern; this signature is notably absent in non-biological objects in motion. By leveraging this characteristic signature alongside the distinction between an object's global movement (extrinsic motion) and the localized movement of its parts (intrinsic motion), we developed an algorithm to measure these traits in tracked objects to determine if they represent a biological entity in locomotion. Additionally, an alternative algorithm based on generic features and machine learning, assembled from related research areas, is presented for comparative analysis. The study provides a novel dataset of biolocomotion featuring a broad spectrum of biological and non-biological objects in natural settings, along with annotations for an existing camouflage animal dataset. Quantitative results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms the alternative approach, validating the hypothesis that biolocomotion can be reliably detected through its unique signature of positional advance with asymmetric oscillation and the disparity between extrinsic and intrinsic motion. Furthermore, analysis of non-biological objects reveals that their motion typically lacks this signature and often exhibits low intrinsic motion relative to extrinsic motion, further supporting the proposed method. Finally, the alternative learning-based algorithm outperforms the proposed approach in controlled laboratory settings with clear backgrounds but struggles when objects move at speeds comparable to typical biolocomotion or when backgrounds are complex and dynamic. Consequently, there has been significant research into fast, approximate iterative methods for matrix inversion accelerated by Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), offering viable alternatives where traditional direct inversion methods are too costly. Existing techniques include the Neumann Series (NS), Newton iteration (NI), Chebyshev Iteration (CI), and Successive Over-Relaxation. This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm derived from the NS, termed "Nested Neumann" (NN). This approach generalizes higher-order iterations of NI and CI by leveraging a computationally efficient iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, dependent on a specified "inception depth." Mathematical analysis confirms that the NN method: (i) converges provided the preconditioning matrix satisfies the spectral norm condition required for NS, (ii) achieves a convergence rate equivalent to an order of (inception depth plus one), and (iii) performs optimally with an inception depth of one or two, contingent upon available RAM. Additionally, we establish an explicit formula for NN, confirming its equivalence to CI for lower depths. Theoretical findings were validated through a numerical example, and practical applications involved solving linear systems and inverting matrices, with results displayed across various dimensions, inceptions depths, and iterations. This work extends previous findings presented in reference [1]. Systems with random scattering exhibit eigenchannels that maximize energy flux through a target area. While these eigenchannels are typically localized near the system boundaries, we demonstrate that in a slab structure containing many random scatterers, some eigenchannels are delocalized and distributed uniformly across the slab. This occurs when the eigenvalue exceeds the average of all eigenvalues, a threshold approximate equal to the system's transmitted average capacity. These principles are broadly relevant to random systems with varying scattering intensities and different wave types, such as electromagnetic waves, matter waves, and acoustic waves.

The fundamental diversity gain in a diverse diversity-division multiplexing system is determined by its eigenchannels, which represent the maximum capacities achievable with specific internal field patterns. We have calculated the eigenvalues and eigenchannels of the diversity matrix derived from the deposition matrix. These eigenchannels reveal how matter wave energy is spatially arranged to define distinct transmission paths within the system. Our results indicate that eigenchannels can be either localized near the boundaries or extend uniformly across the entire structure. These eigenchannels optimize transmission by either preventing matter wave energy from diffracting into opaque obstacle regions or by effectively exploiting such regions. These localized and delocalized eigenchannels correspond to the system's end-fire and broad-side modes, respectively. In this study, we investigate the topological and localization characteristics of a one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model featuring spatially correlated random binary disorder. Our findings reveal that such binary disorder can trigger a transition from a trivial insulator to a topological Anderson insulator across multiple parameter regimes. These topological Anderson insulators are identified by a disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states, observable via the inverse participation ratio in both real and momentum spaces. Furthermore, the boundaries of the topological phases align with analytical predictions derived from the self-consistent Born approximation and the localization length of zero-energy modes. We also examine the influence of bimodal probability distributions on these disorder-induced topological phases and demonstrate that topological signatures can be detected through mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic setups. Ultimately, this work extends the concept of topological Anderson insulators to scenarios involving correlated disorders.

u$ allows us to define a "topological Anderson insulator" within this context. We verify its existence using the anomalous Hall conductance of non-interacting multi-band systems with Gaussian disorder and observe $

Higgs boson production via gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM framework featuring complex parameters. Predictions for the gluon-fusion channel rely on an explicit leading-order cross-section calculation for arbitrary complex parameters, enhanced by higher-order corrections: massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at NLO QCD, top-quark contributions up to N$^3$LO QCD within the heavy top-quark effective theory (including a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs component), and contributions up to NNLO QCD for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component and heavy Higgs bosons. The analysis also incorporates two-loop electroweak effects and interpolates NLO SUSY QCD corrections from the MSSM with real parameters. Finite wave function normalization factors, ensuring correct on-shell properties for external Higgs bosons, are included via the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. For scenarios involving a significant admixture of two heavy Higgs bosons, it is shown that squark effects exhibit strong dependence on the phases of the complex parameters. Theoretical uncertainties regarding the cross sections are discussed, and the results have been integrated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ numerical code named $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. Finally, the computed cross sections for various scenarios are compared with the fundamental parameters of the MSSM. This comparison utilizes data from the fundamental numerical codes $\texttt{SusHiMi}$ and $\texttt{MadGraph5_aMC@NLO}$, employing the two-body 2HDM effective theory with complex parameters as an interpolation tool between scales. These theoretical cross sections for the gluon-fusion process are subsequently used to assess the reliability of existing experimental neutral Higgs measurements at LHC Phase II. Furthermore, the uncertainties and contributions of the underlying perturbative expansions are examined, and the findings are contrasted with the uncertainties of the NNLO bottom-quark annihilation calculation. Finally, an overview of the $\texttt{SusHiMi}$ code is provided, alongside a comparison with other leading-order computational codes featuring real parameters. The work concludes with suggestions for improving both the precision and the parameter space coverage of neutral Higgs-boson production cross sections in future investigations. Code availability is noted.

We derive the asymptotic distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis of linearity and Pitman's local alternatives, covering scenarios where the network dimension remains fixed or grows. In both dimensions, the test follows a standard normal distribution asymptotically under the null. When the network dimension grows, the test can also detect nonlinearity in high-dimensional networks, potentially enhancing power in such contexts. To illustrate the utility of our method, a simulation study is included, followed by an empirical application examining interbank contagion and its impact on loan networks using data from the US Federal Reserve's Supervised Institutions. Additionally, we aim to extend the current framework to accommodate time series regressions that include dynamic network parameters and a low-rank covariance structure, potentially enabling the detection of thresholds in Granger causality. Although standard regression techniques can be adapted to describe non-linear dependencies in network data, they remain suboptimal for capturing the inherently non-linear nature of networks themselves. To address this, we propose a framework for nonparametric regression on graphs, which can be extended to penalized regression and the estimation of conditional conditional density on graphs. To ensure the consistency of these methods, we demonstrate that graph Laplacians must be sufficiently sparse. Furthermore, because nonparametric estimators typically yield biased parameter estimates, a screen-then-estimate procedure is required to recover the $\sqrt{n}$-consistency of the underlying parametric model. Finally, to handle high-dimensional settings, an appropriate screening procedure is necessary.

Consequently, applying classical material mechanics concepts like "rheology" or standard "mechanical response" to cells is insufficient. Instead, a cell functions as a living system where components exhibit reproducible behaviors—such as the contractility of individual stress fibers or the mechanical properties of an actin biopolymer network—yet these constituents reorganize in response to external stimuli in a manner that is neither exactly predictable nor perfectly reproducible. Acknowledging this inherent complexity, this note proposes a multi-physics framework for modeling cell spreading and motility, specifically incorporating the relocation of proteins on advecting lipid membranes. This approach is illustrated using a boundary integral-baseline method, which has been validated against validated data from experiments on red blood cells and root hair cells, as well as simulations derived from more rigorous but computationally demanding methods. It remains an open challenge to apply this model to the broader context of cell motility. Finally, this work highlights the value of a mathematically rigorous yet computationally efficient framework for systematically investigating the link between cellular behaviors and the design of chemical environments, thereby enabling the application of statistical methods to address challenging questions in a stochastic manner. However, this adoption has also allowed cybercriminals to leverage platform vulnerabilities and employ social engineering to target users. While most current detection methods rely on analyzing the transactional behavior of individual wallet addresses, they often fail to examine money trails. This paper proposes a heuristic-based approach that incorporates money trail features to identify suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we focus on cyclic behaviors and detect hidden patterns within temporal transaction graphs, using Ethereum transaction data for demonstration. Our findings reveal that malicious activities—such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering—exhibit distinct cyclic patterns on Ethereum, and we have identified two specific suspicious cyclic path-based transfers. These techniques are adaptable to other cryptocurrency blockchains with suitable modifications tailored to the specific characteristics of the cryptocurrency in question. Numerical and graphical analyses indicate that our method achieves a detection accuracy of approximately 94% on Ethereum data. Consequently, we believe these techniques can assist in identifying malicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains by utilizing money trail information.

surface code currently offers the most viable path to scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computing. Consequently, developing rapid and adaptable decoding algorithms capable of handling faulty syndrome measurements is essential. This study demonstrates that decoding these codes within a full fault-tolerant framework can be naturally recast as repeated interactions between a decoder and its environment, enabling the application of reinforcement learning to train decoding agents. As a proof of concept, we utilized deep Q-learning to create fast decoding agents for the surface code across various noise models. This approach not only tolerant faulty syndrome measurements but also accommodates operations used in logical stabilizer measurements and fault-tolerant data encoding/decoding. Furthermore, we established upper bounds on the duration of decoding frames, providing a framework to train agents on realistically sized circuits. We further explored extending this method to incorporate other properties of error-correction cycles, presenting several strategies for enhancing the agents' error-mitigation performance. Ultimately, we argue that this surface-code-specific model may be generalized to other codes, establishing a foundation for creating practical decoding agents leveraging modern deep learning techniques. This research aligns with the ultimate objective of designing self-correcting quantum computer architectures that function as quantum quantum error-correcting codes, potentially enabling the execution of deep quantum circuits for quantum supremacy and quantum utility. The surface code's flexibility and low operational overhead make it the current top candidate for fault-tolerant quantum computing. The proposed surface-code decoding model is complex, involving a wide range of noise scenarios and operations for error-mitigation, and can be viewed as a quantum circuit in its own right, potentially subject to errors. The general framework for surface-code decoding can address more sophisticated fault-tolerant schemes, and applying error-mitigation techniques to the decoder itself could lower the overhead of error-mitigation. Finally, the presented surface-code decoding model functions as a tool for simulation, and connecting it to a quantum hardware emulator would allow experimental verification of the model's error-mitigation capabilities regarding surface-code correction. We propose this as a significant direction for future work. Surface codes are a leading choice for topological error-correction, and creating self-correcting quantum computers requires handling faulty logical operations and syndrome measurements. The primary contribution of this paper is utilizing a quantum emulator to develop decoding agents using a quantum Markov decision process formulation and deep Q-learning. These agents outperform traditional minimum-weight-match decoders in certain error scenarios while maintaining high correction rates in others, and they do so with significantly lower overhead. No significant alteration in jet fragmentation was detected in $d+Au$ collisions, suggesting that cold nuclear matter effects are negligible. In contrast, hadrons carrying a large momentum fraction from the quark are suppressed in Au+Au collisions relative to $p+p$ and $d+Au$ systems. However, as the momentum fraction decreases, the hadron yield in Au+Au rises to exceed that in $p+p$ collisions. This excess is most prominent at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, particularly for hadrons associated with lower momentum direct photons. Theoretical comparisons indicate that this hadron surplus results from the medium's response to energy deposited by jets. Furthermore, comparing $p+p$ and Au+Au data allows for the direct isolation of jet contributions without relying on perturbative subtractive methods. Consequently, the jet spectrum in Au+Au exhibits stronger suppression than previously indicated, confirming that losing few gluons during traversal leads to significantly fewer hadrons compared to $p+p$ collisions. Finally, data analysis confirms that direct photons serve as an effective background subtraction tool for jets.

In high-energy nuclear collisions, particles originating from hard scatterings form jets, while quarks interacting with the strongly interacting quark-gluon plasma (QGP) undergo inelastic scattering with the medium. This study examines the modification of jet hadronization within the QGP by analyzing the correlation between jets and neutral mesons. Specifically, we investigate the modification of the jet fragmentation function for vector mesons (rho, omega, and phi) by comparing $p+p$ and Au+Au collision data. We observe a significant suppression of low-momentum-fraction hadrons in Au+Au collisions, attributed to jet interactions with the QGP. Additionally, we confirm that the jet contribution to this spectrum is approximately 1.5 times greater than the component arising from medium particles.

computing (HPC) workloads cost-effectively on optimally matched hardware. Nevertheless, despite comparable computational resources between cloud and on-premise HPC environments, their network architectures and performance characteristics can diverge substantially. For instance, the use of distinct network transport and routing protocols in these systems may generate network noise, potentially constraining application scalability. This study examines the network performance, scalability, and economic implications of executing HPC tasks on cloud platforms. The research begins with detailed small-scale measurements focusing on latency, bandwidth, and collective communication patterns, followed by large-scale network performance simulations. Validated across four major HPC and cloud platforms, the findings demonstrate that both network noise and noisy-network effects arise at scales roughly 20 times smaller than those available on-premise, leading to significant cost overruns. Additionally, a model predicting performance and scalability based solely on network parameters is introduced. Consequently, accurate scheduling of HPC workloads requires precise, large-scale performance simulations that incorporate realistic network effects, surpassing the capabilities of models relying exclusively on supercomputer-like ideal networks, shared memory networks, or network-only parameters. These insights are expected to aid application developers and system schedulers in creating more robust workloads and strategies for cloud-based HPC scheduling. Background: Cloud computing is an effective method for accessing the diverse range of HPC architectures and sizes, yet it can present performance challenges due to various cloud deployment factors. Furthermore, the emergence of cost-efficient, commodity cloud services provides access to significant computational capacity, raising the question of how cloud performance compares to traditional HPC systems and the resulting cost implications. Additionally, the performance of massively parallel applications is influenced not only by computational and memory factors but also critically by network performance and the potential for network noise. However, despite the accessible literature on HPC network noise, its presence in clouds and the associated scale at which it occurs remain under-explored. Moreover, there is a scarcity of studies investigating the integration of large-scale network noise into application performance modeling and cost analysis. Finally, various techniques for improving cloud performance have been proposed, though their impact on total cost remains unclear. Significance: This work determines the scale at which network noise appears in clouds, a finding that is 20x smaller than previously reported, and quantifies the corresponding cost overruns. The paper also assesses a model for predicting cloud performance that relies on observable network parameters. This paper addresses a distributed memoryless contextual linear bandit learning scenario where agents observe contexts and select actions, yet are geographically separated from the central learner who performs the optimization without direct access to the contexts. Assuming contexts follow a specific distribution, we introduce a method requiring approximately $5d$ bits per context when the distribution is unknown, and zero bits per context if it is known. This approach achieves a regret bound nearly identical to that of a fully observable setting. Specifically, the bound for the unknown distribution case improves upon existing results by a $\log(T)$ factor (where $T$ is the time horizon), while the bound for the known distribution case reaches information-theoretic tightness. In the unknown distribution case, a complementary adaptive algorithm is proposed to minimize communication without incurring regret penalties. Finally, simulations using common distribution types confirm that our methods significantly outperform existing communication-efficient algorithms. Practical implementations can be found in our open-source repository: https://github.com/Noah-C-Yin/Communicated-LLB.

Communication constraints in wireless networks can severely restrict the performance of contextual linear bandit learning, especially when contexts are high-dimensional. We propose a communication-efficient algorithm that guarantees a regret bound equivalent to the information-theoretic limit of a fully observable system. Our approach involves a two-phase strategy: the initial phase acquires $O(d)$ samples to estimate the context distribution, followed by a second phase where data is transmitted via a communication protocol such as Quantized PCA. We establish the minimax lower bound for this problem and demonstrate the approach's effectiveness across various common distribution types.

We examine a distributed memoryless linear bandit learning environment where multiple agents, located in distant regions, observe contexts and execute actions but cannot directly access the contexts themselves; a central learner collects all observations to perform optimization and update a global model. Although the context dimension $d$ is high, a significant number of features are zero with high probability. In this setup, we establish the minimax regret lower bound for two scenarios differing in the central learner's access to contexts and derive regret bounds for several typical context distribution cases.

Multi-method approaches are increasingly recognized as essential for understanding the complexities of Information Systems. This paper examines the benefits and complexities of employing multiple methods within a single study. It offers a systematic review of recent IS literature (2015–2020) by analyzing 209 articles that utilized multi-method designs. The review highlights the frequent use of quantitative and qualitative methods together, with a predominant focus on quantitative research. While most studies prioritize the development of theory, only a少数 aim to test it. Although the findings confirm that multi-method studies tend to produce significant theoretical outcomes, their primary drawback is the significant time required to conduct them. This underscores the need for researchers to plan their multi-method studies carefully so they can effectively address the complexity of IS phenomena.

Although numerous studies have examined the adoption of Remote Work (RW) and the adoption of Agile (AG), there remains a gap in simultaneously analyzing how these practices influence the adoption of Hybrid Work (HW). To advance models capable of handling negation, we introduce CONDAQA, the inaugural English reading comprehension dataset designed to test a reader's sensitivity to negation. Our approach involves collecting over 16,000 paragraphs by scraping more than 1000 high-quality forum questions from Reddit that explicitly utilize negation. Annealing involves slowly varying Hamiltonian parameters to explore equilibrium phases, making it a powerful method for solving complex optimization tasks. Conversely, quenches entail sudden Hamiltonian changes that drive the system into a non-equilibrium state. This study examines the connection between these two approaches, demonstrating that the critical bottleneck of quantum annealing—the minimum of the annealing gap—can be identified through a dynamical quench parameter characterizing the post-quench quantum state. By integrating statistical methods, such as neural network training, with quench data, we can reconstruct the complete functional behavior of the annealing gap. We further show that insights gained regarding the annealing gap, either partially or fully, enable the design of optimized quantum annealing protocols, yielding practical improvements in time-to-solution. These findings are based on simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians, which model challenging instances of the exact cover problem. Our results indicate that the location of the critical landscape can be readily detected using quench data, suggesting that this landscape is an intrinsic property of the Hamiltonian itself, independent of the annealing process. These landscape properties can therefore be characterized experimentally using only the quantum hardware under annealing control. Additionally, we propose that this landscape can be harnessed to dynamically modify the annealing schedule, potentially applied to current quantum annealers like D-Wave's DW2000E. This strategy generalizes previous static Hamiltonian transformations and can be extended to any Hamiltonian capable of being probed via a single quench parameter. The fundamental principle behind this generalization is that the information encoded in quench data is equivalent to the full spectral density matrix of the annealed Hamiltonian. Consequently, any property of this spectral density matrix can be inferred using quench data.

Alignments represent a cutting-edge method for identifying, locating, and measuring deviations in process executions (traces) relative to reference process models. However, alignments typically require complete process executions that span from start to finish, or at least prefixes of such executions. This paper introduces infix/postfix alignments, outlines methods for their calculation, and assesses their performance using real-world event data. Our findings demonstrate that infix/postfix alignments offer several advantages over traditional end-to-end alignments and their infix/postfix variants, including superior performance on incomplete executions (those not finished) and reductions in both computational complexity and memory requirements, particularly when compared to standard end-to-end alignments. End-to-end alignments require process executions to be complete, or limited to prefixes, but struggle with executions that are neither complete nor prefix-based. In contrast, infix and postfix alignments function effectively with incomplete executions by treating the trace as an extension of the execution. This document explains how to compute infix and postfix alignments using existing methods. Our evaluation indicates that infix/postfix alignments outperform traditional end-to-end alignments in various scenarios. Specifically, they offer advantages over complete executions and prefixes, as well as in calculations involving prefix mining. Furthermore, both approaches allow for the automated discovery of performance indicators and key performance metrics (KPIs) derived from event data, which is difficult to achieve with end-to-end alignments when dealing with incomplete executions.

In this work, we offer a unified theoretical perspective on relational machine learning models capable of addressing these challenges. We establish core definitions, contrast current architectural approaches, and examine performance metrics, datasets, and evaluation protocols. Furthermore, we highlight potential high-impact applications and outline key directions for future research within this field. ### 1Introduction

Machine learning models incorporating relationships among entities are emerging as a emerging solution to pharmaceutical problems involving drug-disease interactions, drug-target associations, and drug-drug interactions (DDIs). These frameworks, often categorized under knowledge graph embedding or graph neural networks, utilize known data such as molecular structures, sequences, attributes, interactions, and indications to enhance predictions of adverse drug events, identify new applications, and develop multi-target therapies.

The field of knowledge graph embedding was formalized in the late 2000s following the creation of the DBPedia project, which structured data from Wikipedia and other sources into a graph format. Since then, numerous machine learning models have been developed to learn from and apply knowledge graphs to graph classification, link prediction, and knowledge base completion tasks.

Although significant advancements have been made in knowledge graph embedding over the past decade, a systematic overview of machine learning models specifically applied to predicting DDIs and multi-drug therapies remains lacking. Our paper addresses this gap by providing a comprehensive survey of existing models, complete with a clickable list of over 500 related papers.

Although performing multiple local updates per iteration before syncing with the PS is a common strategy to alleviate this bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of node-specific data often results in biased models and slow convergence. : We introduce a new consistency regularization technique called interpolation-based consistency (ICT) for semi-supervised medical image segmentation. ICT improves upon existing methods by applying data-adaptive consistency constraints to unlabeled data, leveraging the property that consistency is transitive. Specifically, for an unlabeled image $x$, we define two perturbed versions, $x_a$ and $x_b$, and enforce that the segmentation of the mixed image $x_{\lambda} = \text{mix}(x_a, x_b)$ is consistent with the label of $x_a$ if $\lambda$ is close to $1$, and with the label of $x_b$ if $\lambda$ is close to $0$. This is formulated as a novel GAN-like minimax optimization problem. Experiments on two public cardiac and abdominal pathology MRI datasets confirm our claims and highlight the method's efficiency.

In this work, we utilize graph neural networks to establish a linear relationship between disordered atomic arrangements and the corresponding molecular spectra generated through inelastic electron scattering. This approach allows for the development of efficient spectral-based techniques to assess disorder levels in scattered spectra, a capability that could be essential for evaluating disorder in difficult-to-probe samples using advanced scattering methods like inelastic X-ray scattering. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model models spectral features such as plasmons and Fano resonances, enabling spectral analysis without relying on specific material parameters, which is advantageous for analyzing experimental data. We anticipate that these findings will aid in designing new materials by offering a clearer understanding of how local structural disorder affects electronic and dynamical material properties. We anticipate that the code developed for these models will be made publicly available.

This research addresses a critical challenge in condensed matter physics: analyzing molecular spectra from inelastic electron scattering to determine the degree of disorder in finite, doped, or strained materials. While recent advances in modeling these spectra have enabled the inference of disorder levels, analyzing data for unfamiliar materials remains difficult due to the lack of known material parameters. We present an novel approach leveraging modern machine learning capabilities to overcome these barriers. By employing a lightweight neural network encoder, we can analytically evaluate the spectra of small, slightly disordered molecules and samples.

We anticipate that the code produced for this research will be released openly. Additionally, the studies presented here will advance the analysis of experimental data from various scattering techniques, including inelastic electron scattering (IETS, EELS), double differential Compton profiling, and inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS), facilitating a deeper insight into how a diverse range of disorders influences material performance and lifespan.

Effective machine learning (ML) models for spectral data must capture a system's disorder and complexity. While recent graph neural network (GNN) methods can infer molecular parameters from spectra, they struggle with highly disordered molecules and do not explicitly account for structural complexity. We introduce a novel GNN that explicitly incorporates complexity as a feature, enabling the encoding of increasingly complex molecules. Alongside a traditional GNN, this allows for a new strategy in spectral analysis that explicitly considers both disorder and complexity. We anticipate that these methods will advance the analysis of inelastic electron loss spectra, supporting the measurement of complexity and entanglement in quantum materials.

While deep learning techniques have recently advanced the field of Deep Learning-based Knowledge Tracing (DLKT), the underlying reasons for their success remain unclear, and rigorous evaluation of these methods remains difficult. First, existing data preprocessing steps are often proprietary and custom-tailored, hindering experimental standardization. Second, current DLKT studies frequently employ inconsistent evaluation protocols that lack alignment with real-world educational settings. To resolve these issues, we present \textsc{pyKT}, a comprehensive Python-based benchmark platform designed to ensure valid comparisons across DLKT methods through exhaustive evaluations. The \textsc{pyKT} library features standardized, integrated preprocessing procedures for seven popular datasets across various domains, along with implementations of ten frequently compared DLKT models to facilitate transparent experimentation. Our rigorous, fine-grained empirical studies reveal key insights for effective DLKT, such as how incorrect evaluation settings can cause label leakage and artificially inflate performance, and how many recent DLKT improvements are marginal compared to the initial model by Piech et al. \cite{piech2015deep}. We have open-sourced both \textsc{pyKT} and our experimental data at \url{https://github.com/Zirui-King-Wang/pyKT}, making it a vital resource for future DLKT research.

The \textit{FedBuff} algorithm (Nguyen et al., 2022) mitigates this issue by enabling asynchronous updates that tolerate staleness, thereby improving training scalability while maintaining privacy through secure aggregation. This paper revisits the \textit{FedBuff} algorithm for asynchronous federated learning, extending prior analysis by eliminating boundedness constraints on the gradient norm. It provides a theoretical examination of the algorithm's convergence rate under conditions of data heterogeneity, varying batch sizes, and communication delays. Furthermore, it introduces an enhanced version of \textit{FedBuff}* that supports scalable, heterogeneous, and delay-tolerant training across clients with diverse computing powers and data distributions. Additional insights into communication delay modeling and the connection to FedAvg with varying learning rates are addressed in the supplement. Theoretical claims are rigorously proven across multiple rounds of communication and under varying hyperparameters, including the buffer size $K$. Finally, the extended experimental section evaluates the algorithm's performance on both synthetic datasets and MNIST, comparing its scalability and accuracy against other optimization methods. The overall contribution of this work lies in establishing a solid theoretical framework for the analysis of communication-heterogeneous asynchronous federated learning. In summary, the extended version of this paper offers: (1) a more comprehensive discussion on the bound $M$ representing the number of stale gradients and its impact on convergence; (2) a tighter convergence rate analysis for strongly convex and smooth loss functions, along with a comparison to other algorithms; (3) extended theoretical analysis covering communication and computation heterogeneous settings, along with enhancements to the algorithm and its convergence rate; and (4) a significantly richer experimental section. Specifically, it includes extensions to the communication-heterogeneous analysis on both synthetic and real-world datasets, and the practical considerations behind communication and computation heterogeneity are explored using real-world datasets.

We investigate the convergence of communication-heterogeneous FedBuff, which allows clients to perform different numbers of local updates before sending gradients to the server. Our analysis demonstrates that although a uniform number of local updates (as in standard FedBuff) yields a tighter convergence rate, it may prevent the algorithm from converging when client computing powers are heterogeneous. Consequently, we propose a dynamic local learning rate strategy that ensures convergence for communication-heterogeneous FedBuff at a rate comparable to the fully homogeneous scenario. This approach represents a substantial improvement over communication-heterogeneous FedBuff with a fixed learning rate, as evidenced by evaluations on both synthetic and practical datasets

Transfer learning has been suggested to address these challenges, even when bridging language gaps, such as adapting an English model for German ASR. In this study, we explore transferring an English model to Czech ASR, a task involving languages with lower mutual intelligibility. To streamline this transfer, we introduce the use of an intermediate alphabet—Czech stripped of accents—and demonstrate that this approach is highly effective. This technique also proves beneficial when applied solely to Czech data, resembling a coarse-to-fine training paradigm. Our results show significant reductions in both training time and word error rate (WER). Specifically, training directly on Czech takes 1.5 times longer than utilizing the intermediate representation, while the direct-trained model's WER exceeds that of the intermediate model by 9%. Furthermore, transferring from English to Czech (direct) yields a WER only 7% higher than transferring to the intermediate representation, contrasting sharply with the 40% jump observed without the intermediate step. These improvements are measured against a strong baseline, confirming the robustness of our findings. This paper introduces a novel, diverse social network dataset named "Twitch Gamers," which features multiple potential target attributes. Embedding nodes from heterogeneous information networks often relies on instance attributes, yet the choice of appropriate features remains an open challenge. We introduce an automatic feature selection method designed specifically for this task. The resulting dataset, "Attributes of Heterogeneous Information Network," allows researchers to evaluate and compare novel proximity-preserving and structural role-based node embedding techniques against a standard baseline. These experiments reveal that our proposed feature selection method produces network representations that significantly surpass those of popular state-of-the-art algorithms. Consequently, the Twitch Gamers dataset serves as a practical tool for future research involving node classification and feature selection within heterogeneous information networks.

Although recent methods for generating vector representations of network nodes show promise for various real-world applications, the lack of comprehensive evaluation metrics and benchmark datasets hinders accurate assessment and effective comparison of different algorithms. This paper presents the "Twitch Gamers" dataset, which includes several potential attribute types. We evaluate a proprietary algorithm for node classification on this data, demonstrating that the resulting network representations achieve notably higher accuracy than state-of-the-art methods. These findings establish the Twitch Gamers dataset as a necessary resource for the future assessment and comparison of node embedding techniques and their applications.

Recent advancements in node embedding algorithms promise diverse practical applications; however, the absence of rigorous evaluation metrics and standard benchmark datasets impedes accurate assessment and meaningful comparison among existing methods. We report the creation of the "Twitch Gamers" dataset, which possesses several potential attribute spaces. Our experimental evaluation on this data shows that a specific algorithm for node classification achieves substantially superior accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art approaches. These results highlight the significance of the Twitch Gamers dataset for the future evaluation and comparison of node embedding methods and their potential uses.

Recent studies have incorporated instance attributes into network data to enhance the performance of node embedding algorithms and support downstream tasks like classification. Nevertheless, determining the most suitable feature space remains an unresolved challenge. We propose a multi-objective learning framework that simultaneously constructs network embeddings and performs classification.

The performance of electrified aircraft, characterized as multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems, is compromised when control surfaces lose effectiveness (LE) due to icing, leading to degraded handling qualities and potential loss of control. While extensive literature exists on LE detection and accommodation, often relying on machine learning or data-driven methods, there remains a gap in research regarding the systematic analysis of system-level robustness and the quantification of performance degradation. This work introduces a unified framework for leading LE detection techniques, classifying various sensing errors and introducing a novel performance metric based on control energy. This metric enables the clear quantification of aircraft performance loss and establishes a basis for evaluating robustness across different control scenarios.
The proposed framework is applied to an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) ice accretion database, assessing performance degradation across various ice conditions, magnitudes, and angles

We demonstrate that as the raft undergoes area expansion—driven by the liquid's surface tension—it experiences a critical threshold where it suddenly fractures into multiple smaller segments. This division occurs at a specific particle spacing that represents an optimal configuration for accommodating expansion. ### I. Introduction

Understanding the complex origins of material failure is essential for numerous physical systems. A prominent example is the particle monolayer on an expanding liquid air-water interface, which effectively models dust formation in an oscillating protoplanetary disk or acts as a simplified proxy for dust distribution in quiescent astronomical environments. This monolayer mirrors the conditions found in the stellar atmosphere of a red giant planet, which is thought to be the source of extraterrestrial glass.

In the experiments detailed below, we utilize a particle raft formed by buoyantly suspending particles on an expanding liquid droplet to create a confined system that captures the fundamental principles of material failure. Specifically, we examine particle-laden droplets when they come into contact with fluids possessing both higher and lower surface tensions. This setup is significant because it encompasses a pinning threshold (observed when the surface tension decreases) and a critical failure spacing (occurring upon expansion when the tension increases). These two distinct thresholds share an identical fractional distance from the droplet's center, defined as $r_{\rm pin}/r_{\rm fail} = 0.66 \pm 0.02$. This setup also clarifies the ratchet-like spacing observed in particle rafts during expansion and addresses the position of the first-branching spacings in the fractal patterns generated by dust in quiescent protoplanetary disks.

We analyzed disk dynamics through collisionless-gaseous numerical simulations, which combined direct integration of gravitational interactions for collisionless particles with smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) for gaseous components. Our results indicate that after roughly one billion years, a distinct central bar emerges with a semi-major axis of approximately three kiloparsecs, accompanied by a multi-armed spiral pattern resulting from the superposition of 2-, 3-, and 4-armed spirals. Both the spiral structure and the bar persist for at least three billion years in our simulations. The presence of the Milky Way's bar constrains the density distributions within its subsystems. We determined that a bar fails to form if the disk's radial scale length exceeds 2.6 kiloparsecs, and bar formation is also inhibited by a compact, massive stellar bulge, as anticipated. Furthermore, we show that the peak value observed in the Milky Way's central rotation curve can be attributed to non-circular motions induced by the bar and its orientation relative to the observer. Additionally, the bi-modal radial structure of the Milky Way's outer rotation curve is attributed to dynamical friction between dark matter particles and the multi-component disk. Finally, we argue that certain Milky Way observations previously interpreted as signs of a triaxial halo can alternatively be explained by a axisymmetric halo interacting with a multi-component disk. These findings offer novel insights into the evolution and subsystems of spiral galaxies, as well as specific characteristics of our own galaxy. This study examines the influence of magnetic fields during gas-rich major mergers by conducting high-resolution magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) zoom-in simulations using the Arepo moving-mesh code, alongside hydrodynamic simulations from identical initial conditions. This represents the first cosmologically consistent investigation into how magnetic fields affect major mergers. Unlike previous non-cosmological studies, our results indicate that magnetic fields substantially impact the formation of the merger remnant. While they do not drastically change global characteristics like star formation history, they significantly alter structural properties. The significance of accurate severity classification in COVID-19 chest CT images cannot be overstated, as it directly influences patient treatment plans and prognostic estimates. However, current computer-aided diagnosis systems primarily focus on the binary task of detecting the presence of the virus, neglecting critical granularity in assessing the extent of lung damage and severity grades. Addressing this gap, we propose a novel network that classifies severity into four distinct categories: Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical. This performance improvement stems from IF-CMAC's ability to effectively leverage enhanced input data through the integration of specialized segmentation networks.

We observe that most existing GEC model training datasets hailing from second-language (L2) learning are associated with multiple first languages (L1s). We hypothesize that the linguistic characteristics of a specific L1 account for the model's strong generalization within that particular L1 but result in poor generalization to other L1s. By analyzing the COCOA-L2 tokenco occurrence matrix, we validate this hypothesis and demonstrate the existence of L1-specific latent spaces. Consequently, we develop a cross-lingual GEC model capable of handling multiple L2s and their corresponding native languages. We gather parallel training data across various L1s and employ a cross-lingual embedding layer as the linguistic feature representation. As a result, our model achieves superior performance on L2 GEC tasks while effectively generalizing to new L1s with minimal additional training data.

Although recent advancements in GEC have enabled models to achieve near-native accuracy for L2 languages, they typically underperform on newly learned L1s with low proficiency. This issue arises because current models rely heavily on L1-specific linguistic features, which, while beneficial for GEC, hinder generalization across different L1s. To address this, we propose a dual-encoder neural network that utilizes a cross-lingual attention mechanism. This approach balances the linguistic features of the target L2 with those of a source L1, allowing for improved generalization to unseen L1s without compromising L2 performance

For instance, to analyze changes in suicide-related excess deaths following a national crisis, officials might report a rounded average of death counts before and after the event. among strategic agents with additive valuations, assuming no monetary transfers. In this context, a mechanism is an algorithm that processes agents' reported valuations rather than their true ones. Our primary objective is to determine if mechanisms exist that guarantee the existence of pure Nash equilibria while ensuring fairness in the resulting allocations for all participants. Specifically, we investigate two concepts: envy-freeness up to any one item (EFX) and envy-freeness up to substitution (EFQ). We analyze two scenarios based on the mechanism's capacity to select EFX or EFQ allocations that are also efficient (utilitarianly optimal). Regarding EFX, we affirm that a simple greedy algorithm can always reach a pure Nash equilibrium yielding an EFX allocation. For EFQ, we observe that any mechanism allowing pure Nash equilibria to produce an EFX allocation (such as the round-robin method) can also lead to equilibria resulting in EFQ allocations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any $k \ge 2$, there exists a mechanism with $n^{k+1}$ parameters capable of reaching a pure Nash equilibrium producing an allocation EFX for $2k$ specific items. However, we also establish that for sufficiently large $k$, there are instances involving two items where no pure Nash equilibrium can result in an EFX distribution for those items. Additionally, we explore whether a sub-exponential function of the number of items, $m$, suffices to ensure an EFX allocation for both items and provide an example where an exponential function is necessary. Finally, we prove that an exponential function of $m$ is insufficient to guarantee an EFX up to two items for three agents. When agents have access to an optimal EFX algorithm, we show they can still reach a pure Nash equilibrium producing an EFX up to two items for an exponential number of items $m$. Notably, this result holds even if one agent's values for an exponential number of items are strictly higher than for the remaining items. Such "heavy" agents illustrate a significant limitation of EFX in strategic settings, as an EFX equilibrium does not necessarily yield an EFX up to two items for them. We also establish the insufficiency of weaker fairness criteria, like EFX up to two items, to achieve full EFX fairness. Finally, we offer several additional findings concerning the existence and properties of pure Nash equilibria across various algorithms and fairness metrics. We hope these insights advance the understanding of algorithmic fairness within game-theoretic frameworks.

To investigate the origins and characteristics of this feature, researchers compared new Hα and archival broad-band imaging of UGC 8839 with similar data from four comparable spiral galaxies. The findings suggest that the off-axis star formation in UGC 8839 arises from a hyper-stable, dark matter-dominated disk extending to large galactocentric radii—a configuration that is significantly rare among spirals. Furthermore, the data indicate that this distant star-forming ring is not merely a result of exhaustion in the gas disk but represents a genuine spatial preference for such regions within this specific disk profile. Compared to galaxy samples with lower Sersc index values ($\gamma$), the specific location, brightness, and depth of this ring are markedly distinct. Although the ring is actively forming stars, its surface brightness in both stellar and H$\alpha$ wavelengths is exceptionally faint, causing it to remain undetected in UGC 8839 when observed using standard automated source-finding algorithms. Based on the morphology of this ring and its formation timescales, the dynamical history of UGC 8839 over the last $\sim$1 Gyr appears consistent with a past interaction that was too minor to trigger traditional tidal features or induce conventional interaction-driven star formation. This study offers the first known example of off-axis star formation in a spiral galaxy lacking any obvious recent interaction or disturbance. The peculiar global structure and activity of UGC 8839 provide crucial new insights into the connection between disk stability and star formation, as well as the scaling relations governing the transition from dwarf to massive spirals. searching for dark matter (DM) that differs significantly from the standard approach used in paleo-antimatters. While the majority of DM detection strategies rely on the scintillation of individual particles—typically sub-atomic entities like electrons or nucleons—Palo-detectors aim to observe the ant-dark matter (p-DM) of ancient times through the macroscopic heating of the entire detector volume. This technique relies on a recently confirmed physical mechanism: the coherent scattering of DM off matter nuclei. Because the total heat generated by an ancient p-DM flux is expected to be many orders of magnitude greater than the thermal energy (heat) of a fossilized detector, a substantial signal is anticipated even from very low DM masses (down to $\sim$ GeV/c$^2$), extremely small detector sizes (as small as a few grams), and minuscule interaction cross-sections ($\sim$ pb). This document provides an overview of the Paleo-detector concept, presenting the key theoretical and experimental calculations required to assess the feasibility of actually constructing and utilizing such an instrument. Notably, this method offers the unique advantage of being sensitive to DM-cross sections that are time-dependent and decreasing over time, a characteristic that is highly characteristic of certain dark sector models. Furthermore, the feasibility of Paleo-detectors remains valid even in scenarios involving an evolving universe characterized by a decreasing Hubble parameter and a decaying cosmological constant. Finally, Paleodetectors serve as a powerful tool for precisely determining the temporal behavior of DM-interaction cross sections and related parameters. Although the concept of Paleodetectors was first introduced in a prior publication, this paper expands upon the discussion by addressing various dark matter masses and detector volumes more thoroughly and by incorporating a novel example involving a sub-GeV dark matter particle.

Dark energy constitutes a substantial fraction of the total energy density of the universe. It is conceivable that dark energy comprises a new particle type, the dark photon, which interacts with matter particles—such as nucleons or quarks—via a long-range force analogous to the Coulomb interaction. Although the exact properties of dark energy remain uncertain, its associated interaction range is certainly very long, potentially infinite, and certainly exceeds $10^{-6}$ m. Given the vast number of matter particles within any macroscopic detector volume, the collective weak interactions of ancient dark photons could, in theory, generate a measurable heating effect or a "dark pressure" acting on fossilized detector volumes. Furthermore, we propose the DP-Sync framework, which enhances existing encrypted database schemes to support DP-Sync with DP update patterns. DP-Sync ensures that the complete history of data updates on the outsourced structure remains protected by differential privacy, accomplished through the application of differentially private strategies that govern how data owners synchronize their local data. Our theoretical contributions include a theoretical lower bound on the dimension of the data owner's data, the formal specification of the DP-Sync framework, and an assessment of its practical efficiency. We demonstrate that, for high-dimensional data, DP-Sync outperforms state-of-the-art DP and non-DP schemes with update capabilities in terms of communication costs and execution time. Additionally, we present a real-world scenario involving the non-invasive monitoring of the daily energy consumption of a smart home. This example illustrates that, for medium to high dimensions, the communication requirements of our proposed method are approximately 29.41 times less than those of the most efficient current encrypted database schemes that support data updates. Finally, we examine the non-precise but highly practical situation where the data owner is unwilling to invest the significant communication resources necessary to minimize noise in the summary information. Under this constraint, our experimental results show that the summary data produced by our scheme remains within the accuracy tolerance of non-differentially private methods while maintaining strict compliance with differential privacy. In contrast, the same-tested current encrypted database schemes with update support either fail to produce results within the specified accuracy threshold or cannot generate any results altogether. We also provide a practical bound for the dimension of the high-dimensional data. The various components of our scheme are implemented and integrated into the Extended Elastic Secure Search Framework (ESSF). Our experimental findings indicate that DP-Sync, via the Extended ESSF, is roughly 3.17 times faster than comparable recent non-differentially private search structures capable of handling data with local insert operations. DP-Sync finds applications in scenarios requiring the maintenance of potentially private data owned by a data owner who performs local data inserts, such as energy usage monitoring in intelligent homes, search trends, and data from medical devices like glucose monitors. Our approach, termed Logical Explanation (LExp), is grounded in a new model interpretation model, called RF-MIP, which reformulates an RF to align with the principles of Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) explanations. This allows us to leverage the extensive body of work on mathematical explanations to enhance the interpretability of RFs. The proposed method, Logical Explanation, explicitly identifies the specific features responsible for a prediction. Furthermore, we develop a linear solver algorithm, the Dual Dual Simplex (DDS) solver, to efficiently compute explanations. Experimental results demonstrate that our LExp approach achieves superior performance in terms of both accuracy and keep-out regions compared to leading methods. Additionally, our method offers multi-perspective feature sensitivity analysis, offering a deeper understanding of the classifier's behavior. Extensive numerical experiments confirm that our LExp approach outperforms the leading linear exact solver, yielding higher-quality explanations. Moreover, a benchmark analysis reveals that our model interpretation model, RF-MIP, is significantly more efficient than the generic Generic Superadditive Model (GSAM). Consequently, our LExp approach not only delivers precise explanations but also ensures robust robustness (specifically, keep-out regions), far surpassing that of other existing methods. In terms of runtime, our LExp demonstrates superior efficiency, particularly when explaining High-dimensional (HD) classifiers. Furthermore, the LExp is highly scalable, with runtime remaining constant regardless of the number of trees in the RF or when solving explanation problems for multiple classes in multi-class classification. Finally, we provide a comprehensive feature sensitivity analysis, offering insights into both absolute and relative feature importance. In summary, this method not only generates highly accurate keep-out regions but also delivers a holistic feature sensitivity report, facilitating a comprehensive understanding of RF classifiers. Our findings offer a robust solution for various applications, such as feature selection, sensitivity analysis, and the development of more reliable ML models. In conclusion, our proposed method provides a robust solution for multiple scenarios, including feature selection, sensitivity analysis, and building more reliable ML models.

Despite these gains, challenges remain in detecting and tracking instrument positions. To address this, we assessed and compared popular deep learning methods for automating surgical instrument segmentation in laparoscopy, a crucial step for tool tracking. Our experiments reveal that the Dual decoder attention network (DDANet) outperforms other recent deep learning approaches. On the Robust Medical Instrument Segmentation (ROBUST-MIS) Challenge 2019 dataset, DDANet achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.8739 and a mean intersection-over-union of 0.8183, operating at a real-time speed of 101.36 frames per second, which is essential for such applications. The derived code and weights aim to facilitate future research in automatic instrument position detection and robotics. Although this study represents an initial step, it paves the way for developing more advanced and reliable methods for surgical video analysis. However, the dataset's labeling inconsistencies hinder accurate performance evaluation, as noted in the competition report. Although we are not the sole group working on instrument segmentation, our work represents the most comprehensive evaluation of different deep learning approaches to date. Our findings demonstrate that DDANet, a detailed three-stage design employing dense跳 connections, delivers robust and precise results for both contact and non-contact tools, which was not fully realized by the dataset's original authors. By establishing a solid benchmark for this problem, our work enables the field of surgical instrument detection and robotics to advance at an unprecedented rate. Although we could not specifically measure reliability for clinical applications, our work provides a comprehensive foundation for detecting instrument positions and categories, which is critical for real-world implementation. This research also underscores the significant potential of deep learning in diagnosis and treatment, offering work that is robust, reliable, and innovative.
In conclusion, this study evaluates and compares various deep learning methods for automatic surgical instrument segmentation and detection from video, establishing a benchmark on a publicly available dataset. The findings indicate that DDANet effectively segments all visible parts of the instruments. It is hoped that this benchmark and the comparison of different approaches will inspire future research into reliable real-time detection and tracking for clinical applications, as demonstrated by our robust three-stage design.

While unlabeled surveillance footage is plentiful and easy to acquire, effectively leveraging it to learn meaningful ReID representations remains unclear. Specifically, most existing unsupervised and domain adaptation ReID approaches rely solely on public datasets with limited scales. In this work, we gather a large-scale unlabeled video collection comprising over 102,000 videos and 3,270 images of approximately 1,100 pedestrians, bringing the total dataset to over 1.22 million images. We introduce a novel domain adaptation framework consisting of two stages: first, a semi-supervised pre-training strategy utilizes a small amount of labeled data from the source domain on a large scale of unlabeled source data to learn initial ReID features; second, we develop a cross-domain adaptation technique using only unlabeled target domain data to fine-tune the learned features for accurate identity prediction in the target domain. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on two large-scale cross-domain adaptation datasets. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to explore effective ReID feature learning through large-scale unlabeled video data and to establish a new large-scale cross-domain adaptation ReID benchmark. Our dataset, model, and code are publicly available at https://panqiu2000.github.io/CODA/. The CODA dataset features a comprehensive annotation tool for large-scale person ReID.

analyzing how mass accretion rates correlate with stellar and disk characteristics. While the scatter in these relationships can refine disk evolution models, this is only possible if accretion variability is properly considered. Although variability is significant during the embedded phases of star formation, it is often assumed to be minor in later stages. In this study, we report substantial accretion rate variations observed in the target XX Cha and discuss their implications for population studies of classical T Tauri stars. Comparing mass accretion rates derived from fitting UV-to-near-infrared spectra in recent X-Shooter observations with those measured 11 years prior using the same instrument, we find that XX Cha exhibits nearly 2 dex of accretion variability between 2010 and 2021. While the specific timescales of this variation remain uncertain, XX Cha demonstrates extreme accretion variability for a classical T Tauri star. If such behavior is common among these stars, potentially occurring on timescales longer than previously investigated, it could significantly influence disk evolution models constrained by the observed spread in accretion rates. Finally, we note that earlier studies relying on spectral lines to assess accretion variability may have underestimated the fluctuations in certain targets.
Direct imaging exoplanets remains difficult due to the challenges of separating them from their host stars. Variability induced by cloud cover and instrumental instability hinders the extraction of high-precision astrometric data from direct imaging data, which is essential for separating planetary orbital motion from proper motion and stellar reflex motion (both caused by a planet or the planet's motion around the host star). If direct imaging enables the study of planets forming in protoplanetary disks and those embedded within them, understanding and potentially mitigating the impacts of target variability on astrometric analysis becomes crucial. We illustrate this using high-contrast direct imaging data of XX Cha obtained over nearly a decade. By converting XX Cha's photometric variability into astrometric shifts, we show that even modest levels of photometric variability can result in apparent astrometric jitter that mimics the apparent annual parallax of a nearby system or the amplitude of a planetary signal caused by the planet's orbit around the host star. Consequently, future attempts to detect forming planets via direct imaging and astrometry must account for the variability of both the target star and the instrumentation.

We surveyed a representative U.S. sample, asking participants to make redistribution choices after observing worker outcomes and distinguishing whether luck amplified effort ("lucky opportunities") or directly determined income ("lucky outcomes"). The results show that people reduce their redistribution efforts and become less responsive to shifts in luck's significance when "lucky opportunities" are present. We present a method for influencing reinforcement learning agents by leveraging their reliance on stable data distributions. Our approach involves introducing slight perturbations to the data distribution in a way that is unrecognizable to the agent while having a significant impact on its training process. During training, we utilize a self-play algorithm to continuously generate new data from the progressively updated policy, similarly to how Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) handle data. Although conceptually aligned with recent work on model collapse, our method differs by employing a non-linear classifier instead of a generator. This allows us to control the degree of perturbation and demonstrate that our technique can infiltrate the data distribution more effectively.

This paper investigates data quality issues within ML pipelines by developing methods to assess the difficulty of individual images for a classification model. We begin with a broad definition of difficult images and outline an research program to explore this concept. Subsequently, we present empirical findings from applying various difficulty metrics to the Digits dataset.

while high-order interactions in many real-world complex systems are best represented by hypergraphs, these datasets are frequently released or analyzed only as projections featuring dyadic edges. To comprehend this problem, we first develop a theoretical framework to characterize its implications and worst-case scenarios. This analysis inspires the formulation of a new task: supervised hypergraph reconstruction, which involves recovering a real-world hypergraph from its projected graph by leveraging existing application domain knowledge.

To reconstruct hypergraph data, we begin by analyzing hyperedge distributions within the projection. Based on this analysis, we establish a framework comprising two modules: (1) to manage the vast search space of potential hyperedges, we propose a sampling strategy with efficacy guarantees that drastically reduces the space to a manageable set of candidates; (2) to select the appropriate hyperedges from these candidates, we design a lightweight yet effective hyperedge classifier using projected node features and hyperedge distributions. Extensive experiments confirm our approach's superiority over baselines. Furthermore, we present a real-world case study based on the COVID-100 dataset, demonstrating how our method can uncover hidden community structures and offer insights into proximal node attributes through the projection's node features and links. Finally, we discuss potential extensions of our approach and its relevance to other reconstruction tasks.

First, Shannon entropy calculated from far-field profiles in polar coordinates effectively quantifies emission unidirectionality, overcoming the limitations of previous metrics which fail to remain reliable across varying deformation parameters. Second, while the divergence angle defined phenomenologically via full width at half maximum (FWHM) is difficult to apply to complex peak structures, Shannon entropy derived from semi-marginal probability distributions in Cartesian coordinates yields equivalent results and successfully accommodates even highly intricate emission profiles. Finally, we demonstrate that both approaches are equivalent and apply universally to any probability distribution. This study offers novel perspectives on, and valuable tools for, assessing the directedness of microcavity laser emission. The proposed methods are straightforward to implement and can serve as robust indicators of directionality in future studies, even when spectral structures are highly complex. Determining the conditions under which microcavity lasers exhibit unidirectional emission remains fundamental to advancing their potential applications. This work enhances our capacity to investigate complex spectral structures and difficult cases that were previously challenging to analyze. The introduced methods are broadly applicable to any system where directional emission under specific conditions requires investigation, including all types of confined or resonant systems such as plasmonic lasers, parabolic quantum wells, or metamaser devices. Understanding directionality is essential for determining the optimal geometries and parameter combinations to achieve records in beam directionality and divergence angles. This approach is particularly valuable for exploring novel platform designs, such as coupled microcavity-laser systems, where characterizing directional emission in complex spectral structures is critical for achieving maximum directionality. on deriving effective multi-agent policies from pre-collected datasets, a crucial step for deploying multi-agent systems in real-world scenarios. However, practical applications often involve behavior policies generating joint trajectories with varying performance levels; for instance, one agent might follow a random policy while others adhere to medium-quality policies. In cooperative games with global rewards, existing offline MARL approaches often allow agents to inherit these suboptimal random policies, thereby compromising the team's overall performance. This paper investigates offline MARL with explicit attention to the diversity of individual agent trajectories and introduces a novel framework termed Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) to mitigate this issue. Specifically, an attention-based reward decomposition network utilizes a differentiable key-value memory mechanism to assign credit to each agent in an offline setting. These decomposed credits facilitate the reconstruction of joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay based on individual trajectories, enabling agents to share high-quality experiences. Subsequently, agents conservatively train their policies using a graph attention network (GAT)-based critic. Theoretically, this yields a equilibrium state where the reward decomposition among individual trajectories is optimal, and the resulting policy is as strong as possible given the data. Simulation results confirm that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches. Code is accessible at https://github.com/zhijian7/SIT.

Most conventional intensity-based registration techniques rely on optimization algorithms to maximize image similarity; while these often yield satisfactory results for kilovoltage (kV) images, they struggle with MV images due to inferior image quality and typically lack a sufficient capture range. This paper extends our methodology to achieve motion-corrected radiography for boarders by integrating 3D CT data. We evaluated the system on ten subjects through a phantom study and a formal experiment involving ten minutes of boarder motion. Results indicate that our approach significantly outperforms conventional registration methods. Specifically, combining 2D/3D registration with a CNN achieved motion correction in radiographic images for standing boarders, reducing mean target errors from 13.1mm to 5.3mm (p < 0.001). Additionally, adapting the model to handle various patient postures is straightforward by simply updating the training data.

The proposed motion correction system has been deployed radiography departments at butemaco and Mother and Child Teaching Hospitals in Cambodia. This implementation enables radiologists to produce CT-like images for patients experiencing movement during exposure, thereby improving the diagnosis and treatment of children suffering from drug-resistant malaria.

conference, Einstein proposed a thought experiment aimed at demonstrating the incompleteness of quantum mechanics by leveraging the instantaneous nonlocal consequences of wave function collapse—a phenomenon he termed "spooky action at a distance"—triggered by measurement. This event preceded the famous Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen critique. In this work, we utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how quantum nonlocality actually stems from the fundamental indivisibility of the wave function during collapse. This perspective offers a novel interpretation of the Einstein-Bose effect, which describes an apparent "kick" imparted to unmeasured spin states when one branch of an entangled pair is measured. We show that this effect arises because the spatially separated spin components of a particle function as local probes for the nonlocally connected spins of its partner particle. Consequently, the "kick" experienced by unmeasured spins is not an intrinsic interaction between spins but rather a standard consequence of wave function collapse. Furthermore, this phenomenon explains why the entanglement between spin states remains robust over vast distances and extended time intervals. To validate these claims, we suggest a specific implementation of the thought experiment using the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen inequality. Additionally, we address and resolve the apparent contradiction regarding the entanglement of the particle's position and the "kick" observed in the Stern-Gerlach setup. The proposed thought experiment represents a contemporary realization of the original vision, now feasible thanks to recent technological breakthroughs.

Recently, single photons have been trapped in the axial modes of a paraxial optical cavity, exhibiting nonlocal behavior consistent with quantum entanglement. This nonlocality is reflected in the spatial distribution of the electron cloud surrounding the photon, which changes when a detector at a distant location experiences an avalanche. This nonlocal interaction between the photon and the electron cloud appears to violate local causality, as the influence seems to occur instantly across space. We examine this phenomenon using the parameters of the Cavendish-Coulomb nonlocal interaction model. Our analysis indicates that the observed effects align with a modified version of this model, suggesting that the apparent violation of local causality can be explained by an extremely strong shielding effect occurring between charged particles.

We clarify the nonlocal implications of quantum entanglement using a specific realization of the thought experiment described above. The findings indicate that while the standard form of the Cavendish-Coulomb interaction does not exist in nature, a screened version operates with an infinite range.
